Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for representation learning on graph-structured data. However, traditional GCNs rely on iterative message passing, recursively aggregating information from neighboring nodes. This recursive process can be computationally expensive, particularly for large graphs, and can suffer from oversmoothing, hindering performance. This paper introduces Non-Recursive Graph Convolutional Networks (NR-GCNs), a novel approach that eliminates the recursive message passing mechanism. Instead, NR-GCNs directly learn node embeddings based on precomputed graph features and a carefully designed architecture that captures structural information without iterative aggregation. We demonstrate that NR-GCNs can achieve comparable or even superior performance to traditional GCNs on various graph learning tasks, including node classification and link prediction, while significantly reducing computational complexity and mitigating oversmoothing issues. Our experiments highlight the efficiency and effectiveness of NR-GCNs, offering a compelling alternative to recursive GCN architectures for large-scale graph analysis.
Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) is a challenging task due to the targets' small size, weak signal, and complex background clutter. Existing methods often struggle to effectively capture both local and global contextual information crucial for differentiating targets from noise. This paper proposes a novel Dense Nested Attention Network (DNANet) for robust IRSTD. DNANet leverages a dense nested architecture to facilitate feature propagation and reuse, enriching feature representations at multiple scales. Furthermore, we introduce a nested attention mechanism that adaptively learns to focus on target-relevant features while suppressing background clutter. This attention mechanism is applied within the dense blocks to refine feature maps at each level. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that DNANet achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of detection accuracy, robustness to noise, and visual interpretability, outperforming existing methods in challenging scenarios with complex backgrounds and low signal-to-noise ratios. The proposed architecture effectively balances the need for detailed local information and comprehensive global context, leading to significant improvements in IRSTD performance.
This paper introduces a novel hierarchical self-supervised learning (SSL) framework for medical image segmentation that leverages multi-domain data aggregation.  Addressing the challenges of limited labeled data and domain shift in medical imaging, our approach constructs a hierarchical feature representation by pre-training on a large, diverse collection of unlabeled medical images from multiple domains (e.g., different modalities, anatomical regions, diseases).  The hierarchy is built upon a coarse-to-fine strategy, where initial SSL tasks focus on learning global contextual information across domains, followed by more specialized tasks tailored to individual domains or anatomical regions.  This allows the model to capture both shared anatomical structures and domain-specific characteristics. We employ contrastive learning at each level of the hierarchy to learn robust feature representations.  Experiments on various medical image segmentation tasks demonstrate that our hierarchical SSL method, combined with multi-domain data aggregation, significantly outperforms existing SSL and supervised learning approaches, especially when fine-tuning on limited labeled data from specific target domains.  The results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in improving segmentation accuracy and generalization capability in the presence of domain variations commonly encountered in medical image analysis.
Stochastic binary networks offer advantages in terms of computational efficiency and interpretability, but their training remains a challenge due to the non-differentiable nature of the discrete activation functions. Straight-Through Estimators (STEs) are a popular heuristic used to circumvent this issue, enabling gradient-based learning. However, STEs are often viewed as ad-hoc approximations with limited theoretical justification. This work re-examines STEs within a principled framework, demonstrating how they can be interpreted as approximate solutions to variational inference or reinforcement learning problems. By explicitly formulating the underlying optimization objectives, we provide a theoretical grounding for different STE variants and highlight their inherent biases and limitations. Furthermore, we leverage this understanding to propose novel STE modifications that improve training stability and performance in stochastic binary networks. Our findings suggest that STEs, when viewed through a principled lens, offer a powerful and flexible approach to training these challenging models, and can be further refined to unlock their full potential.
Deep visual saliency models have emerged as powerful tools for predicting human attention in images and videos. These models leverage the representational power of deep neural networks to capture complex image features and their relationship to saliency. This work focuses on understanding and visualizing the inner workings of these models. We explore various techniques for interpreting the learned features, including activation maximization and occlusion sensitivity analysis, to reveal what aspects of the input image drive the model's saliency predictions. Furthermore, we propose novel visualization methods to effectively communicate the model's decision-making process, highlighting the key image regions and feature maps that contribute to the final saliency map. By providing insights into the model's internal representations and decision boundaries, this research aims to improve the interpretability and trustworthiness of deep visual saliency models, ultimately leading to more robust and reliable applications in areas such as image understanding, visual search, and human-computer interaction.
## Abstract: A Statistician Teaches Deep Learning

Deep learning, with its remarkable success in various domains, often feels like a black box to practitioners trained in classical statistical methods. This paper explores the pedagogical approach of teaching deep learning concepts through a statistical lens. By emphasizing the underlying statistical principles, such as parameter estimation, model selection, and regularization, we aim to demystify deep learning and provide a more intuitive understanding of its mechanisms. We demonstrate how traditional statistical concepts like maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian inference, and dimensionality reduction map onto deep learning architectures and training algorithms. Furthermore, we discuss how a statistical perspective can inform the design of robust and interpretable deep learning models, highlighting the importance of error analysis, uncertainty quantification, and causal inference. This approach not only equips statisticians with the necessary tools to engage with deep learning but also offers valuable insights for deep learning practitioners seeking a more principled understanding of their models. Ultimately, we argue that a strong foundation in statistical thinking is crucial for effectively applying and advancing the field of deep learning.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in learning representations for graph-structured data. However, their performance can be limited by issues such as over-smoothing and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies within complex graphs. This paper introduces the Tree Decomposed Graph Neural Network (TDGNN), a novel GNN architecture that leverages tree decomposition to address these limitations. TDGNN decomposes the input graph into a tree structure where each node represents a subgraph of the original graph. This decomposition allows for efficient message passing within and between these subgraphs, enabling the capture of both local and global graph properties. By exploiting the hierarchical structure induced by the tree decomposition, TDGNN mitigates over-smoothing and facilitates the propagation of information across greater distances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TDGNN through experiments on various graph benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in node classification and graph classification tasks compared to existing GNN models. Our results highlight the potential of tree decomposition to enhance the representational power and scalability of GNNs.
Image segmentation, the task of partitioning an image into meaningful regions, has evolved significantly beyond simple pixel-level classification. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of image segmentation and cosegmentation techniques, tracing their development from bottom-up approaches to sophisticated semantic understanding. We explore traditional bottom-up methods that rely on low-level image features like color, texture, and edges, and then delve into more advanced techniques incorporating semantic information. This includes deep learning-based approaches that leverage convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for pixel-wise classification and semantic understanding. Furthermore, we examine the related task of cosegmentation, where the goal is to simultaneously segment common objects or regions across a set of images. The survey highlights key algorithms, datasets, evaluation metrics, and recent advancements in both segmentation and cosegmentation, while also discussing current challenges and future research directions in this rapidly evolving field. By providing a holistic perspective, this work aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking a deeper understanding of the landscape of image segmentation and cosegmentation.
This paper introduces RSS-Net, a novel weakly-supervised multi-class semantic segmentation framework leveraging Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar data. Existing radar-based semantic segmentation methods often rely on expensive and time-consuming pixel-level annotations. RSS-Net addresses this limitation by employing a weakly-supervised learning approach that utilizes only image-level labels for training. The proposed network architecture consists of a radar-specific feature extraction module followed by a multi-class segmentation head. To bridge the gap between image-level labels and pixel-level predictions, we introduce a novel Radar Semantic Similarity (RSS) loss function that leverages the inherent properties of FMCW radar data, encouraging spatially consistent and semantically meaningful segmentation maps. Experimental results on a real-world FMCW radar dataset demonstrate that RSS-Net achieves competitive segmentation performance compared to existing weakly-supervised methods while significantly reducing the annotation burden. This work paves the way for more efficient and scalable deployment of radar-based perception systems in various applications such as autonomous driving and robotics.
This paper presents an advanced image dehazing and haze synthesis technique leveraging the Dark Channel Prior (DCP) enhanced by Multiple Linear Regression (MLR). Traditional DCP-based dehazing methods often suffer from color distortion and halo artifacts. To mitigate these issues, we propose an improved atmospheric light estimation and transmission map refinement using MLR. Specifically, MLR is employed to model the relationship between local image features and the atmospheric light, leading to a more accurate and robust estimation. Similarly, MLR is applied to refine the initial transmission map obtained from the DCP, reducing halo artifacts and improving overall image clarity. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach by utilizing the refined atmospheric light and transmission map parameters to generate synthetic haze on clear images. This allows for controlled experimentation and performance evaluation of dehazing algorithms under various haze conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our MLR-based DCP approach achieves superior dehazing performance compared to traditional DCP methods and other state-of-the-art techniques, producing visually pleasing results with reduced artifacts and improved color fidelity. The generated synthetic haze also provides a valuable tool for benchmarking and training dehazing algorithms.
Deep learning models for nanoparticle segmentation require large, accurately annotated datasets, a significant bottleneck due to the time-consuming and expensive nature of manual annotation. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging synthetic image rendering to address this annotation problem. We demonstrate that training deep learning models on synthetically generated images of nanoparticles, combined with minimal real-world data, achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, segmentation performance compared to models trained solely on extensively annotated real images. Our synthetic data generation pipeline incorporates realistic variations in nanoparticle size, shape, distribution, and background noise, mimicking the complexities of experimental microscopy images. By decoupling the need for exhaustive manual annotation, this synthetic data augmentation strategy offers a scalable and cost-effective solution for training robust deep learning models for nanoparticle segmentation, enabling broader applications in materials science and nanotechnology.
## Move2Hear: Active Audio-Visual Source Separation

This paper introduces Move2Hear, an active audio-visual source separation approach that leverages embodied interaction to improve separation performance.  Traditional audio-visual source separation methods rely on passive observation, often struggling with overlapping sounds and complex acoustic environments. Move2Hear empowers an agent to actively move within the environment, strategically changing its viewpoint to disambiguate sound sources. We propose a novel framework that integrates a reinforcement learning agent with an audio-visual source separation network. The agent learns to navigate the environment, selecting actions that maximize the separability of the target source based on both audio and visual cues. We demonstrate that by actively exploring the environment, Move2Hear significantly outperforms passive audio-visual source separation methods, especially in challenging scenarios with occlusions and strong interference. Our results highlight the potential of embodied perception for enhancing audio-visual understanding and enabling more robust and accurate sound source separation.
Image-based camera localization, the task of estimating a camera's pose from a single image, is crucial for various applications like robotics, augmented reality, and autonomous navigation. This paper proposes a novel approach, a Generative Map, to address the challenges of this task. The Generative Map leverages a generative model to learn a compact and continuous representation of the 3D scene geometry and appearance directly from training images and their corresponding poses. This representation enables the generation of novel views conditioned on a camera pose, effectively creating a differentiable map. During localization, the observed query image is compared to the generated views, allowing for pose estimation through optimization. We demonstrate that this generative approach offers significant advantages over traditional feature-based methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with varying lighting conditions and viewpoint changes. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that our Generative Map achieves competitive accuracy and robustness, highlighting its potential as a powerful tool for image-based camera localization.
Multi-task learning (MTL) has shown promise in improving natural language processing (NLP) tasks by leveraging shared knowledge across related objectives. However, traditional MTL approaches often require significant computational resources and data, hindering their applicability in low-resource settings. This paper introduces a novel **Conditionally Adaptive Multi-Task Learning (CAMTL)** framework designed to enhance transfer learning performance while minimizing parameter overhead and data dependency. CAMTL employs a conditional adaptation mechanism that selectively activates task-specific modules based on input characteristics, thereby enabling efficient knowledge transfer without requiring all tasks to share all parameters. We demonstrate that CAMTL achieves significant improvements in performance across various NLP tasks, including text classification, sequence tagging, and question answering, compared to standard MTL and single-task learning baselines. Furthermore, our experiments show that CAMTL achieves comparable or superior performance using significantly fewer parameters and less training data, making it a more practical and effective solution for transfer learning in resource-constrained NLP scenarios.
Automatic image colorization, the task of adding plausible colors to grayscale images, remains a challenging problem. While deep learning approaches have shown significant progress, many still struggle with preserving fine details and generating vibrant, realistic color palettes. This paper presents a novel approach to automatic image colorization based on an "epitome" representation. Our method leverages a compact, learned representation of the image's underlying structure and color distribution, acting as a holistic descriptor for guiding the colorization process. By encoding key visual elements and their relationships within the epitome, we can effectively propagate colors from a limited set of initial hints or learned priors. We demonstrate that this epitome-based approach allows for more consistent and visually appealing colorizations compared to existing techniques, particularly in preserving texture details and generating harmonious color schemes. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, showcasing its ability to produce high-quality colorizations with minimal user intervention. Furthermore, we analyze the properties of the learned epitome representation and its contribution to the overall colorization performance.
This paper investigates the emergence of compositional language through deep learning agents engaged in a multi-generational language game. We explore how compositional structures, reflecting underlying semantic relationships, can arise from the pressure to communicate effectively across multiple generations. We train a population of sender and receiver agents using a deep neural network architecture, where the receiver must reconstruct the sender's intended meaning based solely on the received message. Crucially, each generation learns from the messages produced by the previous generation, creating a chain of cultural transmission. Our results demonstrate that compositional language, characterized by systematic relationships between message parts and meaning components, emerges as the communication bottleneck tightens and the generational depth increases. We analyze the learned languages and show that they exhibit properties of compositionality, including reuse of message components and systematic generalization to unseen meanings. These findings provide insights into the evolutionary origins of compositional language and suggest that deep generational transmission plays a critical role in shaping the structure of communication systems.
This paper introduces a novel metric designed for comprehensive health analysis, focusing on optimized clustering of health data and robust cross-comparison of results derived from diverse analytical approaches. Current health analysis often relies on traditional metrics that may not fully capture the complex interplay of factors influencing individual and population health. Our proposed metric aims to address this limitation by incorporating a multi-dimensional assessment of health status, weighted according to the specific characteristics of the dataset and the analytical goal. Furthermore, we present an optimization strategy for clustering health data based on this metric, facilitating the identification of distinct health profiles and risk groups. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our metric through a rigorous cross-comparison analysis, evaluating its performance against existing methods and highlighting its ability to provide consistent and insightful results across different analytical frameworks. This research contributes to improved health analysis by providing a more nuanced and versatile tool for understanding and addressing health challenges.
Occluded person re-identification (ReID) is a challenging problem due to the presence of significant occlusions that hinder feature extraction and matching. This paper proposes a novel pose-guided visible part matching approach to address this issue. By leveraging human pose estimation, we identify visible body parts and focus on learning robust features from these unoccluded regions. We introduce a part-aware feature extraction module that utilizes pose information to guide the feature learning process for each visible body part. Furthermore, we propose a visible part matching strategy that selectively compares and aligns features from corresponding visible parts across different person images. This allows us to effectively mitigate the impact of occlusions by focusing on reliable feature correspondences. Extensive experiments on several occluded person ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant performance improvements compared to state-of-the-art methods.
Image captioning, the task of generating natural language descriptions for images, has seen significant advancements in recent years. However, many existing approaches struggle to capture subtle visual details and contextual relationships crucial for generating accurate and informative captions. This paper proposes a novel image captioning model incorporating **context-aware auxiliary guidance** to address these limitations. Our model leverages auxiliary tasks, such as visual relationship detection and attribute prediction, to provide explicit contextual information alongside traditional image features. Crucially, we introduce a context-aware fusion mechanism that dynamically weights the contributions of these auxiliary tasks based on the input image and the current decoding state. This allows the model to selectively attend to relevant contextual cues, leading to more nuanced and contextually appropriate caption generation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, producing captions that are more accurate, descriptive, and semantically coherent. We further provide qualitative analysis to highlight the effectiveness of our context-aware auxiliary guidance in capturing complex visual relationships and generating more informative captions.
Multi-view subspace learning (MVSL) aims to discover a shared latent subspace that captures the complementary information from multiple views of the same data. However, existing MVSL methods often treat each view independently or rely on simple fusion strategies, neglecting the complex inter-view relationships and potentially leading to suboptimal subspace representations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel **Deep Co-Attention Network for Multi-View Subspace Learning (DCAN-MVSL)**.  Our model leverages a deep neural network architecture with a co-attention mechanism to learn view-specific features and dynamically capture the inter-view correlations. Specifically, the co-attention module allows each view to attend to relevant information from other views, enabling mutual enhancement of feature representations. Furthermore, we incorporate a subspace learning layer to project the enhanced view-specific features into a shared latent subspace.  Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that DCAN-MVSL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art MVSL methods in terms of clustering and classification accuracy, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed deep co-attention mechanism in capturing complex inter-view relationships for robust subspace learning.
Crowd-based object segmentation leverages the collective intelligence of multiple annotators to delineate objects within images. However, the quality and consistency of individual annotations can vary significantly, impacting the final segmentation accuracy. This paper introduces a novel approach to crowd-based object segmentation that incorporates clickstream analysis to infer annotator confidence and improve segmentation performance. By analyzing the sequential clicking behavior of annotators during the segmentation process, we extract features indicative of their certainty and expertise. These features are then integrated into a probabilistic framework that weights individual annotations based on their inferred confidence. We demonstrate that incorporating clickstream-derived confidence scores leads to more accurate and robust object segmentation compared to traditional aggregation methods that treat all annotations equally. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset validate the effectiveness of our approach in improving segmentation quality and reducing the impact of noisy or inconsistent annotations.
Multi-image feature matching is crucial for various computer vision tasks like 3D reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and image retrieval. However, processing large image datasets with traditional methods can be computationally expensive and memory intensive, especially when requiring consistent correspondences across all images. This paper presents QuickMatch, a novel distributed algorithm for efficient and consistent multi-image feature matching. QuickMatch leverages a distributed computing framework to parallelize the feature matching process, significantly reducing processing time. Furthermore, it incorporates a robust consistency enforcement mechanism based on cycle consistency and geometric verification to ensure reliable correspondences across the entire image set. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that QuickMatch achieves comparable or superior matching accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while offering significant speedups, making it a practical solution for large-scale multi-image feature matching applications.

Gradient Boosting Trees (GBTs) are powerful machine learning algorithms widely used for prediction tasks. Our results demonstrate that incorporating cross-validation feature selection can lead to more reliable and interpretable feature importance estimates, ultimately enhancing the understanding and applicability of GBT models.
Hierarchical mechanical search, crucial for tasks like assembly planning and robotic manipulation, requires reasoning about both the semantic properties of objects and their geometric relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages 3D scene graphs and neural message passing to effectively model these aspects. We represent a mechanical scene as a graph where nodes encode object semantics and geometric features, while edges capture spatial relationships. Our model employs a neural message passing network to iteratively refine node and edge embeddings by aggregating information from neighboring elements. This allows for learning contextualized representations that encode both object-level understanding and intricate geometric dependencies. These learned representations are then used to guide a hierarchical search strategy, enabling efficient exploration of the solution space for mechanical tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging set of mechanical reasoning problems, showing significant improvements over baseline methods in terms of both accuracy and search efficiency. This work highlights the potential of neural message passing on 3D scene graphs for complex mechanical reasoning tasks.
This paper presents an extended exploration of graph pattern mining and learning, focusing on the crucial role of user-defined relations in both processes. Traditional graph mining often relies on predefined structural patterns or simple adjacency, limiting its ability to capture domain-specific knowledge and complex relationships. We propose a framework that allows users to explicitly define relations between nodes and edges based on their semantic meaning and application-specific context. This enables the discovery of more meaningful and insightful patterns that are relevant to the user's specific goals. We detail the methodologies for incorporating user-defined relations into both graph pattern mining algorithms, allowing for the identification of patterns that satisfy these specified constraints, and graph learning models, enabling them to learn more accurate and generalizable representations that respect the semantic relationships between entities. ## Zoom-In-to-Check: Boosting Video Interpolation via Instance-level Discrimination

Video interpolation aims to synthesize intermediate frames between existing ones, enhancing temporal resolution and enabling slow-motion effects. While existing methods have achieved remarkable progress, they often struggle with complex motion and object occlusions, leading to blurry or artifact-laden results. In this paper, we propose "Zoom-In-to-Check," a novel video interpolation framework that leverages instance-level discrimination to improve the fidelity of generated frames. Our approach focuses on identifying and refining potentially problematic regions with complex motion patterns. We introduce a "Zoom-In" module that crops and magnifies these regions, allowing for finer-grained motion analysis. Subsequently, an "Instance-level Discriminator" assesses the realism and consistency of the interpolated region at the instance level, providing feedback to the generator for iterative refinement. This feedback guides the generator to produce sharper and more accurate details, particularly in areas with intricate motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our "Zoom-In-to-Check" framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art video interpolation methods, achieving superior performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality, especially in scenes with challenging motion and occlusions. The results highlight the effectiveness of instance-level discrimination in boosting the realism and fidelity of video interpolation.

Heterogeneous graphs, containing diverse node and edge types, are ubiquitous in real-world applications. While existing methods often rely on supervised learning or simple unsupervised approaches, they often neglect the rich structural information encoded within meta-paths, which capture semantic relationships between nodes. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNs) have achieved remarkable success in processing graph-structured data. However, traditional GCNs operate in Euclidean space, which may not be optimal for representing hierarchical and complex relationships often found in real-world networks. This paper introduces Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (HGCNs), a novel framework that leverages the properties of hyperbolic geometry to better capture hierarchical structures and latent relationships within graphs. We adapt the core GCN operations, including convolution and aggregation, to operate within hyperbolic space using appropriate Riemannian optimization techniques. By embedding nodes in the hyperbolic space, HGCNs can effectively capture the inherent tree-like structure of many graphs, leading to improved performance on tasks such as node classification and link prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HGCNs through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements over Euclidean GCNs, especially on graphs with pronounced hierarchical organization. Our results highlight the potential of hyperbolic geometry for enhancing graph representation learning and unlocking new capabilities for analyzing complex network data.
This paper presents a complex Knowledge Base Question Answering (KBQA) system designed to leverage multiple reasoning paths for answering complex questions. Current KBQA systems often struggle with questions requiring multi-hop reasoning or incorporating diverse knowledge from a knowledge base. Our system addresses this limitation by employing a modular architecture that explores various reasoning strategies, including path ranking, graph traversal, and semantic parsing. Each module generates candidate answers based on a specific reasoning path. A novel aggregation mechanism then combines these candidates, considering their individual confidence scores and the diversity of their originating reasoning paths. We evaluate our system on a benchmark dataset for complex KBQA, demonstrating significant improvements in answer accuracy and robustness compared to existing approaches. The results highlight the effectiveness of utilizing multiple reasoning paths for tackling the challenges of complex question answering over knowledge bases.
Accurate and explainable cardiac pathology classification from cine Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment planning. This work proposes a novel approach that leverages semi-supervised learning to characterize cardiac motion through apparent flow estimation, subsequently enhancing pathology classification and interpretability. We train a deep learning model to predict apparent flow from cine MRI sequences, utilizing both labeled data with known cardiac pathologies and unlabeled data to improve motion representation learning. The learned apparent flow features are then integrated into a classification model for cardiac pathology identification. Furthermore, we incorporate explainability techniques, such as attention mechanisms and saliency maps, to highlight regions of interest and provide insights into the model's decision-making process based on the estimated motion patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that our semi-supervised apparent flow learning significantly improves the accuracy of cardiac pathology classification compared to traditional methods. The generated explanations offer clinicians valuable information about the underlying motion abnormalities contributing to the predicted pathology, facilitating more informed clinical decision-making. This approach provides a powerful framework for automated cardiac pathology classification with enhanced interpretability, potentially leading to improved diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes.
Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in face recognition, but their performance can be significantly impacted by image degradations commonly encountered in real-world scenarios. This paper investigates the strengths and weaknesses of deep learning models for face recognition when subjected to various image degradations, such as blur, noise, compression artifacts, and illumination variations. We analyze the robustness of different state-of-the-art architectures and training strategies against these degradations, identifying vulnerabilities and resilience factors. Our analysis reveals that while deep learning models can leverage learned features to partially mitigate the effects of some degradations, they remain susceptible to significant performance degradation under severe conditions. Furthermore, we explore potential avenues for improving robustness, including data augmentation techniques, adversarial training, and specialized architectures designed to be invariant to specific types of image degradation. This study provides valuable insights into the limitations of current deep learning approaches for face recognition in challenging environments and highlights directions for future research aimed at developing more robust and reliable face recognition systems.
Reinforcement learning (RL) often struggles with sparse reward environments, particularly when requiring agents to achieve a diverse set of goals. All-goals updates, where experiences are relabeled to be successful for any achieved goal, offer a powerful approach to mitigate this challenge. However, scaling all-goals updates to complex, high-dimensional state spaces remains computationally expensive. This paper proposes a novel architecture leveraging Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to efficiently represent and process state information within an all-goals update framework. By learning spatially aware features from raw sensory input, our approach enables the agent to generalize across different goals and states more effectively. We demonstrate that this CNN-based all-goals update method significantly improves learning speed and performance compared to traditional methods in challenging environments with sparse rewards and complex visual inputs. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior performance on tasks requiring navigation and manipulation, highlighting its potential for scaling all-goals updates to more realistic and complex RL scenarios.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on static image features, our approach analyzes the dynamic characteristics of fingerprint images captured over time. This paper introduces a novel nonparametric variable screening method that leverages optimal decision stumps to identify important predictors in high-dimensional data. Our approach circumvents these limitations by employing decision stumps, simple yet powerful classifiers, to assess the individual predictive power of each variable. This optimal stump-based score is then used to rank variables, enabling accurate selection of relevant features. The proposed approach offers a robust and interpretable solution for identifying key predictors in complex datasets, facilitating downstream analysis and model building.
## AttWalk: Attentive Cross-Walks for Deep Mesh Analysis

Deep learning on 3D meshes has shown promising results in various applications. However, effectively capturing long-range dependencies and complex geometric relationships within mesh structures remains a challenge. This paper introduces AttWalk, a novel deep learning framework for mesh analysis based on **attentive cross-walks**. AttWalk leverages a graph neural network (GNN) architecture to learn node embeddings by aggregating information from neighboring vertices through random walks. Crucially, we introduce an **attention mechanism** that dynamically weights the importance of different cross-walks based on their relevance to the target node. This allows the model to selectively focus on the most informative paths, capturing long-range connections and mitigating the impact of noisy or irrelevant information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AttWalk on several benchmark datasets for mesh classification and segmentation. Our experiments show that AttWalk achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the benefits of attentive cross-walks in capturing complex geometric relationships for deep mesh analysis.
This paper investigates the surprising phenomenon of convergence to global optima in highly overparameterized deep neural networks (DNNs) despite the non-convexity of the training landscape. Panoptic segmentation, the task of simultaneously segmenting and classifying every pixel in an image into both semantic categories (e.g., person, building) and instance identities (e.g., individual people), remains a challenging problem. While fully supervised methods achieve impressive results, they require extensive and costly pixel-level annotations. This paper explores weakly- and semi-supervised approaches to panoptic segmentation, aiming to reduce the annotation burden while maintaining competitive performance. We investigate methods that leverage weaker forms of supervision, such as image-level tags, bounding boxes, or coarse segmentation masks, to train panoptic segmentation models. Our experiments demonstrate that these approaches can achieve significant improvements over existing weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods, bridging the gap between fully supervised performance and annotation cost. This work paves the way for more practical and scalable panoptic segmentation in real-world scenarios with limited labeled data.

Object detection in satellite imagery presents unique challenges due to the high spatial resolution, complex backgrounds, and varying scales of objects. The effective monitoring and management of pandemics require timely and accurate analysis of spatio-temporal data. This paper presents STOPPAGE, a novel cloud-fog-edge computing framework designed to address this challenge. STOPPAGE leverages the strengths of each layer: edge devices collect and pre-process real-time data (e.g., mobility patterns, environmental conditions); fog nodes perform localized data aggregation, filtering, and initial analysis, reducing latency and bandwidth requirements; and the cloud provides large-scale data storage, advanced analytics, and comprehensive visualization for informed decision-making. ## CTAB-GAN: Effective Table Data Synthesizing

Synthesizing high-quality tabular data is crucial for various applications, including data augmentation, privacy preservation, and generating training data for machine learning models. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown promise in this domain, but effectively capturing the complex relationships and distributions within tabular data remains a challenge. This paper introduces CTAB-GAN, a novel GAN-based architecture specifically designed for synthesizing realistic and useful tabular data. CTAB-GAN incorporates techniques for handling mixed data types (numerical and categorical), addressing class imbalance, and learning intricate dependencies between columns. We employ a Conditional Tabular Autoencoder (CTAB) to generate continuous representations of tabular data, which are then used as input to a GAN framework. This approach allows the GAN to learn the underlying data distribution more effectively. We evaluate CTAB-GAN on several real-world datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art table data synthesizers in terms of data fidelity, utility for downstream tasks, and privacy preservation. Our results highlight the effectiveness of CTAB-GAN as a robust and versatile tool for synthesizing high-quality tabular data.
## Abstract: Attacking Optical Flow

Optical flow estimation, a fundamental task in computer vision, provides crucial information for motion understanding and scene analysis. Its applications span autonomous driving, video surveillance, and robot navigation. However, the robustness of optical flow algorithms against adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. This work investigates the vulnerability of state-of-the-art optical flow methods to both white-box and black-box adversarial perturbations. We demonstrate that imperceptible alterations to input images can significantly degrade the accuracy of optical flow estimation, leading to substantial errors in motion vectors. We explore different attack strategies, including targeted and untargeted attacks, and evaluate their effectiveness across various optical flow architectures. Our findings highlight the susceptibility of current optical flow algorithms to adversarial manipulation and underscore the need for developing more robust and secure optical flow estimation techniques for safety-critical applications. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the security limitations of optical flow and paves the way for future defenses against adversarial attacks.
Tree-based classifiers are widely used due to their interpretability and efficiency. However, they often struggle to capture complex relationships between features, particularly when those relationships are not hierarchical. This paper explores a novel classification approach that moves beyond the limitations of trees by explicitly modeling sparse pairwise dependencies between features. Our method learns a classifier that considers a limited number of direct interactions between features, enabling the model to capture more nuanced relationships than traditional tree-based models while maintaining a degree of interpretability. We propose an efficient learning algorithm for identifying and incorporating these sparse dependencies. Empirical results on a variety of datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to tree-based methods and other established classifiers, particularly in scenarios where feature interactions play a crucial role. Furthermore, we show that the learned dependencies can provide valuable insights into the underlying data structure and feature importance.

The acoustic features capture prosodic and spectral characteristics, while the linguistic features represent semantic and syntactic information. These features are integrated within a deep learning framework comprising convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to effectively model complex temporal dependencies and feature interactions. ## Kernel Cuts: MRF meets Kernel & Spectral Clustering

This paper introduces "Kernel Cuts," a novel framework that bridges the gap between Markov Random Field (MRF) based image segmentation and kernel/spectral clustering techniques. While MRFs offer powerful tools for modeling spatial dependencies and enforcing smoothness in segmentation, kernel and spectral methods excel at capturing non-linear data structures and identifying clusters based on similarity. Kernel Cuts leverages the strengths of both approaches by formulating the segmentation problem as a graph partitioning task within a kernel-induced feature space. Specifically, we define a kernel-based affinity matrix reflecting the similarity between pixels based on both their appearance and spatial relationships, incorporating MRF-inspired smoothness terms directly into the kernel. This allows us to perform normalized cuts on the embedded data, effectively minimizing the cut value in the kernel space while simultaneously enforcing spatial coherence. We demonstrate the efficacy of Kernel Cuts on challenging image segmentation datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior performance compared to traditional MRF-based methods and standard spectral clustering algorithms. Our results highlight the benefits of integrating MRF principles into kernel-based clustering for robust and accurate image segmentation.
Private model compression aims to reduce the size and computational cost of machine learning models while preserving both their performance and the privacy of the training data. This paper investigates the use of knowledge distillation (KD) as a mechanism for achieving this goal. We propose a novel framework that leverages KD to transfer knowledge from a large, potentially private, teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student model. Our approach focuses on ensuring differential privacy (DP) during the knowledge distillation process, specifically when generating the soft labels from the teacher model. We explore different DP mechanisms for sanitizing the teacher's predictions and analyze their impact on the student model's performance and privacy guarantees. We demonstrate, through empirical evaluation on various datasets, that our method effectively compresses models while providing provable privacy guarantees, achieving a favorable trade-off between model utility, size, and privacy budget. This work contributes to the growing body of research on privacy-preserving machine learning by providing a practical and effective approach for deploying compressed models in privacy-sensitive applications.
Deep semi-supervised learning leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to train robust and generalizable models. A key challenge lies in effectively utilizing the unlabeled data to guide the learning process. This paper proposes a novel approach to deep semi-supervised learning based on **Metric Learning by Similarity Network (MLSN)**. We introduce a similarity network that learns a metric space where data points with similar features, regardless of label availability, are embedded close together. This similarity network is trained jointly with the main classification network. The similarity network uses unlabeled data to refine the feature representation learned by the classification network, encouraging consistent and meaningful embeddings. By enforcing similarity relationships learned from the entire dataset, the proposed MLSN method improves the generalization performance of the classification network, especially when labeled data is scarce. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements over existing semi-supervised learning methods. The results highlight the benefits of leveraging metric learning to effectively incorporate unlabeled data into the deep learning framework for semi-supervised learning.
This paper investigates the power of multitask representation learning in the context of Linear Markov Decision Processes (Linear MDPs). We consider a scenario where multiple related tasks share a common low-dimensional feature representation, but differ in their reward functions. We analyze how learning a shared representation across these tasks can improve sample complexity compared to learning each task independently.  Our theoretical results demonstrate that by leveraging the shared structure through multitask representation learning, we can achieve significant reductions in sample complexity, scaling with the number of tasks and the dimensionality of the shared feature space. Specifically, we provide bounds on the sample complexity required to learn near-optimal policies for all tasks, highlighting the benefits of transferring knowledge across tasks.  Furthermore, we discuss the conditions under which this transfer is most effective and provide insights into the design of effective multitask representation learning algorithms for Linear MDPs.  Our findings contribute to a theoretical understanding of the benefits of multitask learning in reinforcement learning and provide a foundation for developing more efficient and scalable RL algorithms.
## GazeGAN: Unpaired Adversarial Image Generation for Gaze Estimation

Accurate gaze estimation is crucial for various applications, but its performance heavily relies on large, diverse, and labeled datasets, which are often expensive and time-consuming to acquire. To address this limitation, we propose GazeGAN, a novel unpaired adversarial image generation framework designed to synthesize realistic eye images with controlled gaze directions. GazeGAN leverages a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to translate real eye images into synthetic images with desired gaze vectors, without requiring paired training data. This is achieved by incorporating a gaze-aware discriminator that enforces gaze consistency between the generated images and the specified gaze direction. Furthermore, we introduce a novel loss function that encourages the generator to preserve identity information while manipulating gaze, ensuring realistic and personalized synthetic data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GazeGAN by augmenting existing gaze estimation datasets with our generated images, resulting in significant improvements in gaze estimation accuracy across various benchmark datasets. Our results highlight the potential of GazeGAN as a powerful data augmentation technique for improving the robustness and accuracy of gaze estimation models, especially in scenarios with limited labeled data.
Human action recognition in drone videos presents unique challenges due to varying viewpoints, altitudes, and occlusions. Traditional deep learning approaches often require extensive labeled training data, which is costly and time-consuming to acquire for aerial perspectives. This paper addresses the challenge of human action recognition in drone videos by leveraging a few labeled aerial training examples. We propose a novel approach that combines [**mention the core technique, e.g., transfer learning, meta-learning, or domain adaptation**] to effectively learn from limited aerial data and generalize to unseen scenarios. Specifically, we [**briefly describe the methodology, e.g., pre-train on a large-scale ground-based dataset and fine-tune on a few drone videos, or utilize a meta-learning framework to rapidly adapt to new action classes**]. Experimental results on [**mention the dataset used**] demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in few-shot aerial action recognition, achieving competitive accuracy with significantly less labeled data. This work offers a practical solution for deploying human action recognition systems in resource-constrained drone applications, enabling real-time monitoring and analysis of human activities from an aerial perspective.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown remarkable success in generating realistic data, but their training remains notoriously unstable and challenging. This instability often stems from issues like mode collapse and vanishing gradients. To address these challenges, we propose a novel training algorithm based on Langevin Stein Variational Gradient Descent (LSVGD). Our approach leverages the power of Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) to iteratively update the generator and discriminator distributions towards the optimal solutions, while incorporating Langevin dynamics to enhance exploration and prevent premature convergence to local optima. By approximating the gradient flow on the Wasserstein space with a particle-based optimization, LSVGD promotes diversity and stability in GAN training. We provide theoretical justification for our method and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets. Our results show that LSVGD significantly improves the stability of GAN training, leading to higher quality generated samples and reduced mode collapse compared to traditional GAN training methods and other state-of-the-art stabilization techniques.
Effective response to crisis events requires rapid and accurate understanding of the unfolding situation. Social media platforms serve as valuable sources of real-time information during crises, but their vast and diverse nature necessitates automated methods for categorizing event types. This paper presents a novel approach to multimodal categorization of crisis events in social media, leveraging the complementary information provided by text, images, and potentially other modalities (e.g., video). We propose a model that integrates features extracted from each modality using [mention specific technique, e.g., attention mechanisms, fusion layers]. Our approach aims to overcome the limitations of relying solely on textual data, which can be ambiguous or contain misinformation, by incorporating visual cues and other modalities to improve the accuracy and robustness of crisis event categorization. We evaluate our model on a benchmark dataset of crisis-related social media posts, demonstrating significant improvements in performance compared to unimodal baselines and state-of-the-art multimodal approaches. The results highlight the importance of multimodal fusion for effective crisis event categorization and its potential for enhancing situational awareness and facilitating timely disaster response.
The Image Transformer leverages the powerful self-attention mechanism of the Transformer architecture, originally developed for natural language processing, to address a variety of computer vision tasks. By treating images as sequences of patches, this model eliminates the need for convolutional layers, offering a novel approach to feature extraction and representation learning. This abstract provides a concise overview of the Image Transformer, highlighting its ability to capture long-range dependencies and global context within images, leading to competitive performance on tasks such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. Furthermore, we discuss the benefits of using a self-attention based architecture, including its inherent parallelization capabilities and its ability to learn task-specific representations directly from data. The Image Transformer represents a significant shift in the landscape of computer vision, offering a promising alternative to traditional convolutional neural networks.
In-vehicle object detection is a critical component for the safe and reliable operation of driverless vehicles, enabling them to perceive and understand their surrounding environment. However, deploying robust object detection systems in real-world scenarios, often referred to as "in the wild," presents significant challenges due to the inherent variability in lighting, weather conditions, object appearance, and the complexity of urban environments. This paper addresses the problem of in-vehicle object detection in the wild, focusing on improving the performance and robustness of deep learning-based object detectors under challenging conditions. We explore novel techniques for data augmentation, domain adaptation, and robust feature extraction to enhance the detector's ability to generalize to unseen environments and handle adverse conditions. Furthermore, we investigate methods for efficient inference to ensure real-time performance on embedded platforms within the vehicle. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches in improving object detection accuracy and robustness, paving the way for more reliable and safer driverless vehicle navigation in complex real-world environments.
## Don't Miss the Mismatch: Investigating the Objective Function Mismatch for Unsupervised Representation Learning

Unsupervised representation learning aims to learn meaningful data representations without relying on labeled data. While various objective functions have been proposed, a crucial aspect often overlooked is the potential mismatch between the objective function optimized during training and the downstream tasks where the learned representations are ultimately utilized. This mismatch can lead to suboptimal performance, even with seemingly well-trained models. This work investigates the objective function mismatch problem in unsupervised representation learning. We systematically analyze the relationship between different pre-training objective functions and their impact on downstream task performance across a range of datasets and architectures. Through empirical analysis, we demonstrate how the inherent biases introduced by specific objective functions can hinder generalization to certain tasks. Furthermore, we propose metrics for quantifying the degree of objective function mismatch and explore strategies for mitigating its effects, including multi-objective learning and adaptive objective function selection. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the downstream task during the design and evaluation of unsupervised representation learning methods, ultimately advocating for a more holistic approach to representation learning that bridges the gap between pre-training objectives and real-world applications.
This work provides a comprehensive analysis of exact inference in graphical models using the degree-4 Sum-of-Squares (SoS) hierarchy. We investigate the power and limitations of this relaxation for solving key inference tasks, including marginal inference, maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference, and constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) on various classes of graphs. By leveraging recent advances in SoS lower bounds and algorithmic techniques, we establish precise conditions under which the degree-4 SoS relaxation can provably achieve exact solutions. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of the computational complexity of inference in graphical models and offer insights into the trade-offs between approximation accuracy and computational cost when using SoS-based approaches. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for specific graph structures and provide concrete examples illustrating the strengths and weaknesses of the degree-4 SoS hierarchy for exact inference.
Medical image analysis often involves processing volumetric data, where each volume is composed of a series of 2D slices. Existing representation learning methods for medical images often treat the entire volume as a single entity, neglecting the inherent structure and relationships between individual slices. In this work, we propose a novel approach, "Learning Slice-Aware Representations with Mixture of Attentions," to explicitly model these inter-slice dependencies. Our method employs a mixture of attention mechanisms, where each attention head focuses on different aspects of the slice relationship, such as local context, global context, and specific anatomical structures. By combining the outputs of these diverse attention heads, we generate slice-aware representations that capture richer and more informative features compared to traditional volume-based approaches. We evaluate our method on [mention specific medical imaging tasks, e.g., organ segmentation, disease classification] using [mention datasets, e.g., CT scans of the liver, MRI scans of the brain]. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves performance compared to baseline methods, highlighting the effectiveness of explicitly modeling inter-slice dependencies for learning robust and discriminative representations in medical image analysis.
Flow-based anomaly detection leverages the inherent properties of network flows to identify unusual or suspicious activities within a system. By analyzing patterns in network traffic, such as volume, source-destination pairs, and protocol usage, this approach can detect anomalies that deviate from established baseline behaviors. This abstract presents a general overview of flow-based anomaly detection, highlighting its advantages in terms of scalability and real-time analysis. It explores common techniques employed, including statistical modeling, machine learning algorithms, and knowledge-based rule systems, to characterize normal network behavior and flag deviations indicative of anomalies. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges and future directions of flow-based anomaly detection, focusing on improving accuracy, reducing false positives, and adapting to evolving network environments. This approach offers a valuable tool for enhancing network security and identifying potential threats.
We introduce Holopix50k, a large-scale, diverse stereo image dataset captured "in-the-wild" using the Looking Glass Portrait holographic display. Existing stereo datasets often suffer from limitations such as restricted environments, synthetic content, or limited real-world diversity. Holopix50k addresses these shortcomings by providing over 50,000 stereo image pairs representing a wide range of subjects, lighting conditions, and scene complexities. The dataset includes accompanying metadata such as capture location, date, and time, facilitating research into domain adaptation and generalization. We detail the data acquisition process, describe the dataset's characteristics, and provide baseline results for disparity estimation using established stereo matching algorithms. Holopix50k is publicly available to the research community and aims to accelerate advancements in stereo vision, depth estimation, novel view synthesis, and other related areas, particularly for applications targeting holographic display technologies.
Graph-structured data is ubiquitous across diverse domains, yet effective learning from such data often relies on manually engineered features and architectures. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning representations from unlabeled graph data, but the design of effective SSL strategies and architectures remains a challenging task requiring significant expert knowledge. This paper introduces an automated approach for self-supervised learning on graphs. Our method leverages automated machine learning (AutoML) techniques to automatically discover and optimize graph augmentation strategies, pretext tasks, and encoder architectures tailored to the specific characteristics of the input graph data. We explore a search space encompassing various graph augmentation techniques, including node attribute masking, edge perturbation, and subgraph sampling, combined with diverse pretext tasks such as node property prediction and graph structure reconstruction. Furthermore, we automate the selection and configuration of graph neural network (GNN) architectures. Experimental results on a variety of graph datasets demonstrate that our automated approach achieves significant performance improvements compared to manually designed SSL methods and standard GNN baselines, highlighting the potential of AutoML to democratize and enhance graph representation learning.
Warfarin is a widely prescribed anticoagulant with a narrow therapeutic index, making accurate dosage estimation crucial to avoid adverse events. Traditional methods rely on clinical factors and pharmacogenetic information, often requiring iterative adjustments and patient monitoring. This work explores the application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) to develop an intelligent agent capable of estimating personalized warfarin dosages. We propose a novel RL framework where the agent learns an optimal dosage policy by interacting with a simulated patient population, receiving rewards based on the achieved International Normalized Ratio (INR) target and penalties for deviations. The agent utilizes patient features as state information and selects dosage adjustments as actions. We evaluate the performance of the RL agent against existing dosage algorithms and demonstrate its potential to achieve improved INR control, reduced time to stabilization, and personalized dosage recommendations, ultimately contributing to safer and more effective warfarin therapy.
## AdaBins: Depth Estimation using Adaptive Bins

Monocular depth estimation aims to infer per-pixel depth from a single image, a challenging task due to the inherent ambiguity of monocular vision. This paper introduces AdaBins, a novel approach to depth estimation that leverages adaptive bin discretization to improve performance and robustness. Instead of relying on uniformly spaced bins or regressing depth directly, AdaBins dynamically adjusts the bin ranges based on the scene context. This adaptive binning strategy allows for a more nuanced representation of depth, particularly in regions with high depth variance. Our architecture employs a transformer-based encoder to extract rich image features, followed by a decoder that predicts bin locations and confidence scores. The final depth map is then reconstructed by combining these predictions. Extensive experiments on standard datasets demonstrate that AdaBins achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing existing methods in accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different binning strategies and show that adaptive binning significantly contributes to improved performance, especially in challenging scenarios with complex geometry and varying lighting conditions.
This paper addresses the challenging problem of few-shot segmentation of 3D shapes. Existing methods often struggle to generalize to novel categories with limited training examples. To overcome this, we propose a novel "Learn to Learn Metric Space" approach. Our method learns a high-quality metric space where the distance between 3D shape features accurately reflects semantic similarity. Specifically, we employ a meta-learning framework that trains a metric embedding function to map 3D shape points into a feature space optimized for few-shot learning. During training, we simulate few-shot segmentation tasks and learn to adapt the metric space based on limited support examples. This adaptation allows the model to effectively generalize to unseen categories at test time. We evaluate our approach on challenging 3D shape segmentation benchmarks and demonstrate significant improvements over existing few-shot learning methods, showcasing the effectiveness of learning a task-adaptive metric space for 3D shape segmentation.
This paper introduces equivariant wavelets, a novel approach to constructing wavelet scattering transforms (WSTs) that are explicitly equivariant to both rotations and translations. Traditional WSTs offer robustness to deformations and invariance to translations, but lack explicit rotational equivariance, limiting their effectiveness in applications where orientation information is crucial. Our method leverages group representation theory to design wavelets that transform predictably under rotations, ensuring that the resulting scattering coefficients reflect the rotated input signal accordingly. This equivariance enables faster computation of rotationally invariant features by reducing the need for extensive averaging over orientations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by developing a fast, rotation and translation invariant WST based on these equivariant wavelets. We present experimental results showcasing the improved performance and computational efficiency of our equivariant WST compared to standard WSTs in tasks requiring rotation awareness, such as texture classification and object recognition.
Knowledge graphs (KGs) are crucial for representing structured knowledge, facilitating tasks like question answering and link prediction. Embedding methods aim to represent KG entities and relations in a low-dimensional space, enabling efficient reasoning and computation. Traditional KG embedding models typically operate in real-valued vector spaces. However, these models often struggle to capture complex relation patterns like symmetry, antisymmetry, and composition. This paper introduces Quaternion Knowledge Graph Embeddings (QKE), a novel approach that leverages the properties of quaternions to represent entities and relations. Quaternions, with their four components, offer richer representational capacity and can naturally encode rotational relationships. QKE represents entities and relations as quaternion vectors and employs a quaternion-based scoring function to measure the plausibility of triples. We demonstrate that QKE effectively captures complex relation patterns and outperforms state-of-the-art KG embedding models on standard benchmark datasets for link prediction, showcasing the advantages of using quaternion algebra for knowledge graph representation.
## Grid-to-Graph: Flexible Spatial Relational Inductive Biases for Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often struggle with tasks requiring reasoning about spatial relationships between objects, particularly in environments with varying object layouts and complexities. This paper introduces "Grid-to-Graph," a novel approach to injecting flexible spatial relational inductive biases into RL agents. Grid-to-Graph leverages a learnable mapping from the grid-based visual representation of the environment to a graph structure. This graph explicitly represents objects as nodes and their spatial relationships as edges, allowing the agent to reason about the environment in a more structured and relational manner. The mapping is learned end-to-end with the RL policy, enabling the agent to adapt the graph representation to the specific task at hand. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Grid-to-Graph on a suite of challenging navigation and manipulation tasks with varying object configurations and complexities. Results show that agents equipped with Grid-to-Graph significantly outperform baseline methods that rely on raw pixel input or fixed graph representations, exhibiting improved generalization and sample efficiency. This work highlights the importance of flexible relational inductive biases in enabling RL agents to learn robust and efficient spatial reasoning.
## Abstract: Predictive Inequity in Object Detection

Object detection models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications, making it crucial to understand their potential for unfairness. This paper introduces the concept of "predictive inequity" in object detection, focusing on the differential performance of these models across subgroups defined by sensitive attributes like race, gender, or socioeconomic status. We argue that while overall performance metrics may appear acceptable, significant disparities can exist in the detection accuracy, localization precision, and confidence scores for objects associated with different subgroups. We explore potential sources of predictive inequity in object detection, including biases in training data, algorithmic biases within model architectures, and variations in object appearance across subgroups. Through empirical analysis on benchmark datasets and controlled experiments, we demonstrate the existence and magnitude of predictive inequity in state-of-the-art object detection models. Finally, we discuss potential mitigation strategies and highlight the need for fairness-aware evaluation and development practices to ensure equitable deployment of object detection systems.
This paper explores a novel approach to image captioning by integrating rule-based entity masking. Traditional image captioning models often struggle to accurately describe the relationships between objects in complex scenes. We propose a system that leverages rule-based entity masking to pre-process images, highlighting specific entities based on predefined rules. This masked image, along with the original, is then fed into a captioning model. By explicitly focusing the model's attention on key entities identified by the rule-based system, we aim to improve the accuracy and relevance of generated captions, particularly in describing the interactions and attributes of these entities. We evaluate our approach on benchmark datasets, demonstrating that integrating rule-based entity masking leads to improved caption quality, especially in scenarios requiring detailed descriptions of specific object relationships. Our findings suggest that combining symbolic reasoning with data-driven learning offers a promising direction for enhancing image captioning performance.
Trajectory prediction in traffic scenes is crucial for autonomous driving and advanced driver-assistance systems. Existing approaches often struggle to effectively model the complex spatial relationships between agents and the intricate channel-wise dependencies that influence their future movements. This paper introduces a novel Spatial-Channel Transformer Network (SCTN) designed to address these challenges. SCTN leverages a spatial transformer module to capture the dynamic interactions between agents by attending to their relative positions and movements within the scene. Furthermore, a channel transformer module is incorporated to model the interdependencies between different feature channels representing various aspects of agent behavior, such as speed, heading, and acceleration. By effectively fusing spatial and channel information, SCTN learns a more comprehensive representation of the traffic scene and significantly improves trajectory prediction accuracy. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SCTN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to predict realistic and accurate trajectories in complex traffic scenarios.
This paper explores the problem of identifying the original, full-sized image from which a given sub-image (patch) was extracted. We propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based approach to address this challenging task. Our method learns to map sub-images to their corresponding full image representations by leveraging the inherent spatial relationships and contextual information within the image data. The network architecture is designed to effectively capture features that are indicative of the sub-image's location and content within the original image. We investigate different CNN architectures and training strategies to optimize performance on this task. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in accurately identifying the original image from a sub-image, even in the presence of variations in scale, rotation, and noise. This research has potential applications in various fields, including image forensics, content-based image retrieval, and image editing.
Anomaly detection in the electrical grid is crucial for maintaining system reliability and preventing cascading failures. This paper presents a dynamic graph-based approach for identifying anomalous behavior in the grid. We represent the electrical grid as a dynamic graph, where nodes represent grid components and edges represent their interconnections. This dynamic graph evolves over time, reflecting changes in power flow and network topology. Our method leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn normal operational patterns from historical data. By comparing real-time graph embeddings generated by the GNN with learned normal patterns, we can identify deviations indicative of anomalous conditions. The dynamic nature of the graph allows us to capture temporal dependencies and adapt to evolving grid conditions. We evaluate our approach on real-world electrical grid data and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting various types of anomalies, including cyberattacks, equipment failures, and operational errors. The results show significant improvements in anomaly detection accuracy and reduced false positive rates compared to traditional methods.
The ongoing debate regarding the superiority of Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) and Transformers for visual representation learning motivates this study. We investigate the transferability of representations learned by ConvNets and Transformers across diverse downstream tasks. Specifically, we evaluate and compare the performance of features extracted from pre-trained ConvNets (e.g., ResNet, EfficientNet) and Transformers (e.g., ViT, DeiT) on a range of visual tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. By analyzing the transfer learning performance, we aim to determine which architecture yields more generalizable and transferable visual representations. Our findings provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture and contribute to a deeper understanding of the characteristics of effective visual representations for downstream tasks, ultimately informing the selection of appropriate pre-trained models for various applications.
Arbitrary-shaped text spotting, which aims to detect and recognize text instances of any shape in natural images, remains a challenging task due to the complexity of representing and processing irregular text geometries. This paper presents PAN++, an enhanced version of the Pixel Aggregation Network (PAN) designed for efficient and accurate end-to-end spotting of arbitrarily-shaped text.
