Building upon PAN's strengths, PAN++ introduces several key improvements, including a refined aggregation module for more precise text region delineation, a novel feature enhancement strategy leveraging contextual information, and optimized training techniques for faster convergence and improved robustness. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PAN++ achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed, showcasing its effectiveness in handling complex text layouts and challenging image conditions. The proposed enhancements significantly improve the efficiency and reliability of end-to-end arbitrary-shaped text spotting, paving the way for more practical applications.
Molecular representation learning aims to encode chemical structures into informative numerical vectors for downstream tasks like property prediction and drug discovery. While traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features or graph-based neural networks, recent advancements in language models (LMs) present a compelling alternative. This work investigates the potential of "reprogramming" pre-trained LMs for effective molecular representation learning. We explore techniques to adapt LMs, originally trained on text corpora, to understand and process molecular data. Specifically, we focus on strategies for encoding molecules as sequences (e.g., SMILES strings) and fine-tuning LMs to capture crucial chemical information. We evaluate our reprogrammed LMs on a diverse set of benchmark datasets, demonstrating their ability to generate high-quality molecular representations that outperform existing methods in predictive accuracy and generalization capability. Our findings highlight the promise of leveraging the power of pre-trained LMs for molecular representation learning, offering a flexible and efficient approach to tackle challenging problems in cheminformatics and related fields.
Regression tasks often suffer from limited and imbalanced datasets, hindering model generalization. Data augmentation techniques can alleviate this issue, but naively mixing existing data points may lead to suboptimal performance. This paper introduces MixRL, a novel data augmentation framework for regression that leverages Reinforcement Learning (RL) to intelligently mix existing data points. MixRL trains an RL agent to dynamically select data pairs and determine the optimal mixing coefficients for each pair based on the predicted impact on the target variable. By learning to create augmented data points that effectively improve model training, MixRL enhances the diversity and representativeness of the training dataset. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MixRL across various regression tasks, showing significant improvements in predictive accuracy and robustness compared to traditional data augmentation techniques and state-of-the-art regression models. Our results highlight the potential of RL-driven data augmentation for addressing data scarcity challenges in regression problems.
Large-scale Transformer-based models, such as BERT, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various natural language processing tasks. However, their significant computational cost and memory footprint hinder their deployment in resource-constrained environments. This paper presents a case study on compressing BERT, exploring various techniques to reduce its size and inference time while minimizing performance degradation. We investigate methods including knowledge distillation, pruning, and quantization, analyzing their individual and combined effects on model size, speed, and accuracy. Our findings provide insights into the trade-offs between compression rate and performance, offering practical guidance for deploying efficient BERT models in real-world applications. This work contributes to the ongoing effort of making powerful Transformer models more accessible and usable across a wider range of platforms.
PointGoal navigation, the task of navigating to a target location specified by its 3D coordinates in an unseen environment, remains a challenging problem for embodied agents. This paper investigates the use of auxiliary tasks to accelerate and improve learning in PointGoal navigation. We propose a novel approach that incorporates auxiliary tasks focusing on environment understanding and action prediction. Specifically, we train the agent to simultaneously predict scene depth and semantic segmentation, alongside predicting future actions. By leveraging these auxiliary objectives, the agent develops a richer understanding of the environment and learns more effective navigation strategies. We demonstrate through extensive experiments in simulated environments that our proposed auxiliary task learning framework significantly improves the sample efficiency and overall performance of PointGoal navigation agents compared to baselines trained without auxiliary tasks. Our results suggest that learning auxiliary tasks provides valuable inductive biases, enabling faster and more robust adaptation to unseen environments.
Adversarial patch attacks pose a significant threat to the robustness of deep learning models in image recognition. While effective, many existing patch attacks are visually conspicuous, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. This paper explores the generation of visually imperceptible adversarial patches on digital images. We propose a novel approach that minimizes the perceptual impact of the patch while maintaining its adversarial effectiveness. Our method leverages perceptual similarity metrics and frequency domain manipulation to craft patches that are nearly indistinguishable from the original image, even under close scrutiny. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark image classification datasets, showcasing its ability to reliably mislead state-of-the-art models with minimal visual artifacts. The results highlight the vulnerability of deep learning systems to subtle adversarial perturbations and emphasize the need for robust defenses against visually imperceptible attacks.
Log files are ubiquitous in modern software systems, providing valuable insights into system behavior, performance, and security. However, the inherent variability in log file formats poses a significant challenge to automated analysis. Traditional log parsing methods often rely on rigid regular expressions or pre-defined templates, which struggle to adapt to evolving log structures and require significant manual effort. This paper proposes a novel approach to flexible log file parsing using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). Our method automatically learns the underlying structure of log files by modeling the sequence of tokens as a Markov process. By training HMMs on unlabeled log data, we can infer the hidden states representing different log message types and subsequently extract key parameters without requiring prior knowledge of the log format. We evaluate our approach on diverse real-world log datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately parse logs with varying structures and noise levels, outperforming traditional template-based methods in terms of adaptability and robustness. This HMM-based approach offers a promising solution for automated and flexible log analysis, enabling efficient extraction of valuable information from complex and evolving log data.
Low-bit quantization is a promising approach for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. However, aggressive quantization often leads to significant accuracy degradation. This work proposes a novel learnable companding quantization (LCQ) method to mitigate this issue. LCQ introduces a learnable companding function that non-linearly maps the original full-precision activations and weights before quantization. This allows for a more efficient distribution of quantization levels, concentrating them in regions of high data density and reducing quantization error. By jointly optimizing the companding function and the network parameters, we achieve significantly improved accuracy compared to conventional uniform and non-uniform quantization schemes, especially at ultra-low bitwidths. Experiments on various benchmark datasets and network architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed LCQ method in achieving competitive or superior performance while maintaining significant memory and computational savings. We show that the learned companding function effectively adapts to the data distribution, leading to more accurate and robust low-bit neural networks.
Data augmentation is a crucial technique for improving the generalization ability of neural image classification models. This paper proposes a novel data augmentation strategy that leverages K-means clustering to construct multiple auxiliary tasks that promote feature learning and improve classification performance. Our method first extracts features from intermediate layers of a pre-trained network. These features are then clustered using K-means, and each cluster is treated as a distinct auxiliary task. By training the original classification network to simultaneously predict the original label and the cluster assignments (auxiliary tasks), we encourage the network to learn more robust and discriminative features. We demonstrate that our approach effectively regularizes the network, mitigates overfitting, and ultimately leads to significant improvements in image classification accuracy on several benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different K-means configurations and feature extraction layers to provide insights into the optimal design of this augmentation strategy.
Detecting adversarial examples remains a critical challenge for deploying robust machine learning models. This paper proposes a novel unsupervised approach for identifying adversarial examples that leverages model explanations. Our method avoids the need for labeled adversarial data by analyzing the inherent characteristics of model explanations generated for both clean and potentially adversarial inputs. We hypothesize that adversarial perturbations, even subtle ones, can significantly alter the patterns and stability of model explanations. We introduce a suite of metrics to quantify these alterations, focusing on the complexity, entropy, and sensitivity of explanations. By applying unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to these explanation-based features, we effectively identify data points exhibiting anomalous explanatory patterns, indicative of adversarial manipulation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across various datasets and model architectures, showing that it can effectively detect adversarial examples without requiring any prior knowledge of the adversarial attack or labeled data. This provides a valuable tool for proactively identifying and mitigating adversarial threats in real-world applications.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are typically trained to minimize a divergence between the generated and real data distributions. However, this view is often interpreted as a requirement for the divergence to decrease at every training step. This work challenges this assumption, demonstrating that GANs can successfully converge to a generator that produces realistic samples even when the estimated divergence fluctuates and, at times, increases during training. We present theoretical and empirical evidence showing that convergence in GANs is not solely dependent on monotonic divergence reduction. Instead, we argue that the dynamics of the discriminator and generator interaction, including the ability to escape local minima and explore the parameter space, are crucial for reaching a satisfactory equilibrium. Our findings suggest that focusing solely on minimizing divergence as a training objective may be overly restrictive and that exploring alternative training strategies that allow for transient divergence increases could potentially lead to improved GAN performance and stability.
Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged as a computationally efficient alternative to traditional NAS methods by training a single, large "super-network" encompassing all candidate architectures and evaluating architectures based on shared weights. However, a significant "optimization gap" persists, where the performance ranking of architectures within the super-network often deviates substantially from their performance when trained independently. This discrepancy hinders the effectiveness of weight-sharing NAS. This work investigates the key factors contributing to this optimization gap and frames the problem as a "battle" between the super-network's ability to accurately represent individual architectures and the inherent limitations imposed by weight-sharing. We analyze the impact of architectural diversity, training strategies, and evaluation metrics on the gap, proposing novel techniques to mitigate its effects. Our findings demonstrate that by carefully addressing these factors, we can significantly shrink the optimization gap, leading to improved architecture search performance and more robust NAS solutions.
Anchor-based object detectors are widely used in computer vision, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various detection tasks. However, they are susceptible to a phenomenon we term "Momentarily Missed Detection" (MMD), where objects are consistently missed in a short sequence of frames despite being present and detectable. This paper analyzes the underlying causes of MMD, identifying key factors related to anchor assignment, feature representation, and Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) instability. We propose a novel solution, [**Insert brief, impactful description of the proposed solution, e.g., a temporal smoothing mechanism for anchor assignment and NMS optimization**], designed to mitigate the impact of these factors. Experimental results on [**Mention relevant datasets, e.g., COCO and KITTI**] demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces MMD, leading to improved object detection accuracy and robustness, particularly in video sequences and scenarios with rapid object motion or occlusion. Our findings provide valuable insights into the limitations of anchor-based detectors and offer a practical solution to enhance their performance in real-world applications.
Accurate segmentation of skin lesions in dermoscopic images is crucial for automated diagnosis and monitoring of melanoma and other skin cancers. This paper proposes an enhanced convolutional-deconvolutional network architecture for improved dermoscopic image segmentation. Our approach builds upon traditional U-Net models, incorporating enhancements such as [mention specific enhancements, e.g., attention mechanisms, residual connections, dilated convolutions] to improve feature extraction and boundary delineation. These enhancements aim to address challenges inherent in dermoscopic images, including low contrast, artifacts, and variations in lesion appearance. We evaluate the performance of our proposed network on a publicly available dermoscopic image dataset, demonstrating significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to baseline U-Net and other state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results show that our enhanced network achieves higher Dice scores, Intersection over Union (IoU), and other relevant metrics, suggesting its potential for assisting dermatologists in more accurate and efficient skin lesion analysis.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are notoriously difficult to train, often suffering from instability and mode collapse. This paper introduces a novel approach to improve GAN training by combining probability ratio clipping and sample reweighting. We address the discriminator's tendency to overpower the generator by clipping the probability ratio between real and fake samples, preventing excessively confident predictions that can lead to vanishing gradients for the generator. Furthermore, we introduce a sample reweighting scheme that prioritizes challenging and informative samples during training, focusing the discriminator's attention on regions of the data distribution where the generator struggles. By adaptively adjusting the weights based on the discriminator's confidence, we encourage the generator to address its weaknesses more effectively. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets that our proposed method stabilizes GAN training, improves sample quality, and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing GAN training techniques.
Time-series representation learning aims to extract meaningful and compact features from sequential data for downstream tasks. This paper introduces a novel approach, Temporal and Contextual Contrasting (TCC), for learning robust time-series representations. TCC leverages contrastive learning to capture both temporal dynamics and contextual information within time-series data. Specifically, temporal contrasting encourages representations of temporally proximal segments to be similar while pushing apart representations of distant segments, capturing the sequential dependencies. Simultaneously, contextual contrasting learns to distinguish between representations of different time-series instances by contrasting each instance against a set of negative samples drawn from other time-series. This joint optimization of temporal and contextual relationships leads to representations that are sensitive to temporal patterns and discriminative across different time-series. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TCC on a variety of time-series classification and forecasting tasks, showing that it outperforms existing unsupervised representation learning methods in capturing relevant features and improving downstream performance.
## Abstract: Style Transfer With Adaptation to the Central Objects of the Scene

Existing style transfer methods often apply stylistic changes uniformly across an entire image, potentially neglecting the semantic importance of central objects. This can lead to visually jarring results where important elements are rendered in a way that disrupts their recognizability or aesthetic appeal. To address this limitation, we propose a novel style transfer approach that incorporates adaptation to the central objects of the scene. Our method identifies and segments these central objects, allowing for a more nuanced application of stylistic changes. Specifically, we leverage [mention key techniques, e.g., attention mechanisms, semantic segmentation, object detection] to control the degree of style transfer applied to these regions. By carefully modulating the stylistic influence based on the object's semantic role and visual characteristics, we can preserve important details and maintain visual coherence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, showing that our method produces style transferred images with improved visual quality and better preservation of central object identity compared to state-of-the-art methods. This results in more aesthetically pleasing and semantically meaningful style transfer outcomes.
This paper introduces "Funnelling," a novel ensemble method for heterogeneous transfer learning, specifically designed to address the challenges of transferring knowledge across diverse feature spaces. Funnelling leverages a combination of multiple pre-trained models, each trained on potentially different source tasks and feature representations, and systematically filters and combines their predictions to optimize performance on a target task. This process is analogous to a funnel, where diverse inputs are filtered and channeled towards a focused output. We apply Funnelling to the challenging problem of cross-lingual text classification, where models trained on resource-rich languages are used to classify text in resource-poor languages. Experimental results demonstrate that Funnelling significantly outperforms existing transfer learning approaches in cross-lingual text classification tasks, showcasing its ability to effectively integrate heterogeneous knowledge and achieve state-of-the-art performance. The method's adaptability and strong empirical results highlight its potential for a wide range of heterogeneous transfer learning applications.
## Abstract: Microtubule Tracking in Electron Microscopy Volumes

Reconstructing cellular architecture at the nanoscale requires accurate segmentation and tracking of key structural components. Microtubules, dynamic cytoskeletal filaments crucial for various cellular processes, are often challenging to analyze in large-scale electron microscopy (EM) volumes due to their density, tortuosity, and potential for ambiguity. This work presents a methodology for robust and automated microtubule tracking within EM volumes. We leverage advanced image processing techniques, including [mention key techniques like anisotropic filtering, edge detection, or machine learning-based segmentation], to identify and delineate microtubule cross-sections. A graph-based approach is then employed to connect these cross-sections across consecutive slices, allowing for the reconstruction of individual microtubule trajectories. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on [mention the type of EM data used, e.g., serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBFSEM) data of neuronal tissue], showcasing its ability to accurately track microtubules over significant distances and in complex cellular environments. This automated tracking pipeline provides a powerful tool for analyzing microtubule organization and dynamics in situ, facilitating a deeper understanding of their role in cellular function and disease.
Image captioning aims to generate descriptive and coherent sentences that accurately represent the visual content of an image. Evaluating the quality of these generated captions remains a challenging task. Existing metrics often focus on n-gram precision or recall against human-generated references, which may not adequately capture the nuances of semantic similarity and human consensus. This paper introduces CIDEr (Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation), a novel metric that directly assesses the consensus between a generated caption and a set of reference captions. CIDEr employs Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) weighting to capture the importance of different n-grams within a corpus of image descriptions. By comparing the cosine similarity of TF-IDF vectors representing the generated and reference captions, CIDEr effectively measures the degree to which a generated caption aligns with the prevailing consensus among human descriptions of the image. We demonstrate that CIDEr correlates significantly better with human judgments of caption quality compared to existing metrics, highlighting its effectiveness in evaluating image description models. Furthermore, we show that optimizing image captioning models using CIDEr as a reward function leads to improved performance as perceived by humans.
This paper introduces a novel approach to motif discovery and word segmentation using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) that can process variable-length input sequences. Traditional SOMs require fixed-length input vectors, limiting their applicability to tasks involving sequences of varying lengths, such as biological sequence analysis or natural language processing. Our method addresses this limitation by employing a dynamic programming strategy to align and compare variable-length input sequences, generating a fixed-length feature vector suitable for training a standard SOM. This allows the SOM to cluster sequences based on underlying patterns and similarities, regardless of their specific length. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two distinct tasks: motif discovery in biological sequences and unsupervised word segmentation in natural language. Results show that our variable-length SOM achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods, offering a flexible and efficient framework for uncovering recurring patterns and segmenting sequences into meaningful units without requiring prior knowledge of motif length or word boundaries.
Learning decision-making policies from logged interaction data is a common approach, particularly when real-world experimentation is costly or impractical. However, such data often contains inherent biases that can significantly impact the performance of learned policies. This paper focuses on the impact of discretizing continuous variables within logged interaction data on the resulting policy learning. We argue that discretizing logged features, while seemingly simplifying the data, introduces biases that can disproportionately affect certain actions or states. These biases arise from the information loss inherent in discretization and the potential for skewed representation of different action-state combinations within the discretized space. We theoretically analyze how discretization can distort the true underlying relationships in the data and lead to suboptimal policies. Furthermore, we empirically demonstrate, through simulations and real-world datasets, that discretization can significantly degrade the performance of learned policies compared to using continuous representations, highlighting the importance of careful consideration of data preprocessing techniques when learning decision-making policies from logged interaction data.
## Channel-wise Knowledge Distillation for Dense Prediction

Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a powerful technique to transfer knowledge from a large, complex teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student model. While traditional KD methods often focus on distilling global features or final predictions, they may overlook the fine-grained, channel-specific knowledge crucial for dense prediction tasks. This paper proposes a novel channel-wise knowledge distillation method specifically designed for dense prediction problems such as semantic segmentation and object detection. Our approach distills knowledge at the channel level by aligning the feature representations of the teacher and student networks on a per-channel basis. We introduce a channel-wise attention mechanism to highlight the most informative channels in the teacher's feature maps, guiding the student to focus on learning the most relevant knowledge. Furthermore, we employ a channel-wise similarity matching loss to encourage the student to mimic the relationships between channels in the teacher's feature space. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing KD techniques and achieves state-of-the-art performance for dense prediction tasks. This highlights the importance of channel-wise knowledge transfer in capturing fine-grained details and improving the accuracy of student models in dense prediction scenarios.
System identification, the process of building mathematical models of dynamical systems from observed data, is a crucial task in various engineering and scientific disciplines. This paper explores the application of Gaussian Processes (GPs) as a powerful non-parametric Bayesian approach to system identification. GPs offer several advantages, including the ability to capture complex, non-linear relationships, quantify uncertainty in model predictions, and seamlessly integrate prior knowledge. We review the theoretical foundations of using GPs for system identification, focusing on different kernel choices and their impact on model performance. Furthermore, we discuss various GP-based identification strategies, including direct identification, equation error methods, and state-space modeling. The paper highlights the strengths and limitations of GPs in system identification compared to traditional parametric methods, emphasizing their ability to handle high-dimensional and complex systems. Finally, we present examples demonstrating the effectiveness of GP-based system identification in diverse applications, showcasing their potential for improved model accuracy, robustness, and uncertainty quantification.
This study presents a comparative analysis of various statistical skin detection algorithms applied to a dataset of human images representative of the Sub-Continental population. Accurate skin detection is crucial for numerous applications including face detection, gesture recognition, and content-based image retrieval. However, challenges arise due to the diverse skin tones and complex lighting conditions prevalent in Sub-Continental imagery. This research evaluates the performance of established statistical methods, such as Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Bayesian classifiers, in distinguishing skin from non-skin pixels. Performance metrics including precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy are used to assess the effectiveness of each algorithm. The results highlight the strengths and limitations of each method in the context of Sub-Continental skin tone variations and provide insights into optimizing skin detection for improved performance in this specific demographic. The findings contribute to the development of robust and culturally sensitive image processing applications.
Vehicle tracking in urban environments presents significant challenges due to occlusions, varying lighting conditions, and the dynamic nature of traffic flow. This paper proposes a novel vehicle tracking system leveraging surveillance camera networks and multimodal data fusion to enhance tracking accuracy and robustness. Our approach integrates visual data (RGB images/video) with supplementary information from other modalities, such as license plate recognition (LPR) and vehicle make and model recognition (VMMR). This fusion strategy addresses limitations inherent in relying solely on visual features by incorporating contextual and identifying information. Specifically, we employ a Kalman filter framework for tracking, augmented by a data association algorithm that intelligently fuses visual features with LPR and VMMR outputs. Experimental results on real-world surveillance footage demonstrate that the proposed multimodal fusion approach significantly improves tracking performance compared to methods based solely on visual data, particularly in scenarios with frequent occlusions and challenging lighting conditions. This work offers a promising solution for robust and reliable vehicle tracking in complex urban environments, enabling applications such as traffic monitoring, security surveillance, and intelligent transportation systems.
## Abstract: The Potential of the Return Distribution for Exploration in RL

Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often struggle with efficient exploration, especially in sparse reward environments. Traditional exploration strategies primarily focus on state-action visitation counts or uncertainty quantification in value estimates. This work proposes leveraging the **return distribution** – the probability distribution over possible cumulative rewards – as a novel signal for exploration. We argue that the shape and characteristics of the return distribution, beyond its mean, provide valuable information about the uncertainty and potential for higher rewards in different state-action pairs. Specifically, we explore how metrics derived from the return distribution, such as variance, skewness, and kurtosis, can be used to guide exploration towards regions of the state-action space with high uncertainty and potential for significant improvements in performance. We present preliminary results demonstrating that incorporating these distribution-based exploration signals can lead to improved sample efficiency and faster learning compared to conventional exploration methods, particularly in challenging environments with sparse or deceptive rewards. This research highlights the potential of the return distribution as a rich source of information for driving effective exploration in RL.
This paper presents a novel RGB-D SLAM system designed to operate robustly in dynamic environments. Utilizing point correlations between consecutive RGB-D frames, we explicitly identify and mitigate the influence of moving objects on the map building and pose estimation processes. Our approach leverages a combination of geometric and appearance features to establish reliable point correspondences, followed by a robust outlier rejection strategy based on motion consistency. Points identified as belonging to dynamic objects are down-weighted during optimization, minimizing their impact on the estimated camera trajectory and the reconstructed static scene. We evaluate our system on challenging RGB-D datasets featuring significant dynamic elements, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing SLAM methods in dynamic environments. The results highlight the effectiveness of our point correlation-based approach for decoupling static scene reconstruction from the disruptive effects of moving objects, ultimately enabling more reliable and accurate SLAM performance in real-world scenarios.
Achieving systematic generalization, the ability to apply learned skills to novel situations with compositional variations, remains a significant challenge for deep reinforcement learning (DRL). This paper proposes a novel approach to address this challenge by integrating Task Temporal Logic (TTL) with DRL. We leverage TTL to formally specify task goals, enabling a structured representation of compositional task variations. Our method trains a DRL agent to satisfy TTL specifications, promoting the learning of reusable skills and their compositional structures. By encoding task goals in a formal language, we facilitate the transfer of learned knowledge to unseen tasks with different temporal requirements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a set of complex, compositional tasks, showcasing its ability to generalize to novel task variations with significantly improved performance compared to traditional DRL methods and other generalization techniques. Our results suggest that explicitly representing task temporal structure with TTL, coupled with DRL, provides a promising avenue for achieving robust systematic generalization in reinforcement learning.
Accurate segmentation of anatomical structures in medical volumes is crucial for diagnosis, treatment planning, and image-guided interventions. However, variations in image acquisition parameters and patient anatomy across different modalities pose significant challenges. This paper introduces a novel approach for translating and segmenting multimodal medical volumes using a Cycle- and Shape-Consistency Generative Adversarial Network (CS-GAN). Our CS-GAN leverages cycle consistency to learn bidirectional mappings between different modalities, enabling the generation of synthetic images that retain essential anatomical information. Furthermore, we incorporate a shape consistency loss that encourages the generated images to maintain the shape characteristics of the original images, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. The proposed method allows for leveraging information from multiple modalities to improve segmentation performance, even when one modality is missing or of poor quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on [mention specific dataset(s) if applicable, e.g., brain MRI and CT scans], showing significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the potential of CS-GAN for accurate and robust multimodal medical image analysis.
Data fusion aims to combine information from multiple sources to achieve a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of a phenomenon. However, traditional data fusion techniques can be computationally expensive, hindering their applicability in resource-constrained environments. This paper presents a novel approach to lightweight data fusion using conjugate mappings. We leverage the properties of conjugate functions to efficiently transform and combine data from heterogeneous sources, minimizing computational overhead while preserving essential information. By mapping source data into a shared domain via conjugate transformations, we enable simple and effective fusion operations, such as averaging or weighted averaging. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results on [mention specific application domain, e.g., sensor networks, image processing, etc.], showcasing significant reductions in computational complexity compared to existing methods, while maintaining comparable or improved fusion accuracy. This lightweight approach facilitates data fusion in resource-limited applications, opening possibilities for real-time and embedded systems.
This paper introduces a novel "Plug-in, Trainable Gate" designed to streamline arbitrary neural networks by dynamically controlling information flow. Existing methods for network pruning and compression often require extensive retraining or introduce significant architectural changes. Our approach offers a flexible and minimally invasive solution: a learnable gate that can be seamlessly inserted into existing network architectures. This gate, implemented as a lightweight module, learns to selectively forward or block information based on the input, effectively deactivating redundant or less impactful connections. Crucially, the gate is end-to-end trainable alongside the original network, allowing for efficient adaptation and optimization of the network's computational graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across diverse network architectures and datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model size and inference speed while maintaining or even improving accuracy. Our results highlight the potential of plug-in, trainable gates as a powerful tool for automated network streamlining and efficient deployment of complex neural networks.
Large motion in video sequences poses a significant challenge for video super-resolution (VSR) due to severe misalignment and blur. This paper introduces a novel VSR framework, termed "Large Motion Video Super-Resolution with Dual Subnet and Multi-Stage Communicated Upsampling," designed to effectively address this issue. Our approach employs a dual subnet architecture: one subnet focuses on motion estimation and compensation to align frames, while the other aims to reconstruct high-frequency details. To handle large displacements, we propose a multi-stage communicated upsampling module. This module progressively refines the reconstructed resolution through multiple upsampling stages, exchanging information between adjacent stages to ensure consistency and reduce artifacts. Specifically, the output of each stage is communicated to both the subsequent stage and the final reconstruction module, enabling a more robust and accurate upsampling process. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art VSR algorithms, particularly in scenarios with significant motion, achieving superior performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality.
This paper proposes a novel graph-based approach for approximating the geodesic distance on statistical manifolds, with application to multimedia information retrieval (MIR). Calculating the exact geodesic distance, a crucial metric for comparing probability distributions represented as points on a manifold, is often computationally prohibitive. Our method constructs a graph representation of the manifold, where nodes correspond to data points and edges are weighted based on local similarity. By leveraging shortest path algorithms on this graph, we efficiently estimate the geodesic distance between any two distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach within the context of MIR, specifically for content-based image and audio retrieval. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that our graph-based geodesic distance approximation achieves comparable accuracy to computationally expensive methods while offering significant speed improvements, leading to enhanced retrieval performance. This work offers a practical and scalable solution for harnessing the power of geodesic distances in various statistical manifold learning applications, particularly in the realm of multimedia analysis.
This paper proposes a novel approach for logo detection, leveraging a Discriminative Semantic Feature Pyramid Network (DSFPN) with Guided Anchoring. The DSFPN enhances the standard Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) by incorporating discriminative semantic information at each pyramid level, enabling the network to better distinguish logos from cluttered backgrounds and similar objects. This is achieved through [mention specific mechanism, e.g., attention mechanisms or semantic segmentation]. Furthermore, we introduce a Guided Anchoring strategy that learns to predict the optimal location and shape of anchors, effectively addressing the challenges posed by varying logo aspect ratios and scales. This guided anchoring mechanism improves recall by reducing the reliance on pre-defined anchor boxes. Experimental results on [mention datasets, e.g., Logo-32, FlickrLogos-32] demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in logo detection, surpassing existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. The combination of DSFPN and Guided Anchoring significantly improves the robustness and precision of logo detection, making it a promising solution for real-world applications.
Geometric registration of medical images is crucial for various clinical applications, enabling comparison and integration of multi-modal or longitudinal data. Traditional registration methods often rely on visual features, which can be susceptible to variations in image intensity, contrast, and noise. This work explores the potential of deep learning-based registration without explicitly extracting visual features. We investigate the limits of registration accuracy achievable by training deep neural networks to learn direct mappings from image coordinates to deformation fields, effectively bypassing feature extraction. Our approach utilizes only spatial information derived from the image grid itself, allowing the network to learn implicit geometric relationships between images. We evaluate the performance of our proposed method on a variety of medical imaging modalities and demonstrate the attainable accuracy, highlighting the potential for robust and efficient registration even in the absence of reliable visual features. This study provides insights into the fundamental geometric information encoded within medical images and demonstrates the capability of deep learning to leverage this information for accurate and feature-agnostic registration.
## Faster-LTN: A Neuro-Symbolic, End-to-End Object Detection Architecture

Object detection, a crucial task in computer vision, often struggles with reasoning and incorporating prior knowledge. This paper introduces Faster-LTN, a novel neuro-symbolic object detection architecture leveraging Logic Tensor Networks (LTNs) to enhance performance and interpretability. Faster-LTN builds upon a Faster R-CNN backbone, augmenting it with an LTN layer that enforces logical constraints and incorporates symbolic knowledge about object relationships and scene context. This end-to-end trainable architecture allows for seamless integration of neural perception and symbolic reasoning. We demonstrate that Faster-LTN achieves superior performance compared to traditional object detection models, particularly in scenarios with limited data or complex relationships between objects. Furthermore, the LTN layer provides insights into the model's reasoning process, improving transparency and enabling more reliable predictions. Our results showcase the potential of neuro-symbolic approaches for object detection, offering a pathway towards more robust, interpretable, and knowledge-aware vision systems.
Deep neural networks are known to be vulnerable to adversarial examples, raising concerns about their robustness and generalization capabilities. This paper investigates the impact of adversarial training on the transferability of deep models, specifically focusing on image classification tasks. We hypothesize that adversarial training not only improves robustness but also leads to better feature representations that generalize more effectively to unseen datasets. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that adversarially-trained models exhibit significantly improved transfer learning performance compared to standardly-trained counterparts, even when transferring to datasets with differing distributions. Our findings suggest that adversarial training acts as a regularizer, forcing the model to learn more robust and transferable features, thereby enhancing its ability to adapt to new and potentially adversarial environments. This work provides compelling evidence for the benefits of adversarial training beyond robustness, highlighting its potential for improving the overall generalization and transferability of deep learning models.
This paper explores the integration of logical specifications of objectives within the framework of Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL). Traditional MORL often relies on scalarized reward functions or Pareto front approximations to guide the learning process. However, this can be limiting when dealing with complex, non-linear preferences or when objectives are best expressed through logical relationships. We propose a novel approach that allows agents to learn policies that satisfy objectives defined using temporal logic, specifically Linear Temporal Logic (LTL). By translating LTL formulas into reward shaping functions, we enable the agent to directly optimize for the satisfaction of these logical constraints alongside other numerical objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments in diverse environments, showcasing the ability to learn policies that adhere to complex temporal goals while simultaneously optimizing for multiple quantitative rewards. Our results suggest that incorporating logical specifications provides a more expressive and intuitive way to define and achieve desired behaviors in MORL, leading to more interpretable and controllable learning outcomes.
## Cycle-IR: Deep Cyclic Image Retargeting

Image retargeting aims to adapt an image to a different aspect ratio or resolution while preserving its visual content. This paper introduces Cycle-IR, a novel deep learning framework for image retargeting that leverages a cyclic consistency loss to ensure high-quality and content-preserving results. Unlike traditional methods that often rely on heuristics or local operations, Cycle-IR employs a cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) architecture. This allows the model to learn bidirectional mappings between different aspect ratios, forcing the retargeted image to be reconstructible to the original image through an inverse mapping. This cyclic constraint significantly reduces artifacts and distortions typically associated with image retargeting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Cycle-IR through extensive experiments on various datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual assessment compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Our results highlight the benefits of cyclic consistency in achieving robust and visually pleasing image retargeting.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in this domain, they often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies and global contextual information. Transformers, with their self-attention mechanism, offer a potential solution to address these limitations. This paper introduces the Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMT), a novel architecture designed specifically for medical image segmentation. PMT leverages a hierarchical pyramid structure to extract multi-scale features, effectively capturing both local details and global context. Specifically, we integrate transformer blocks within each pyramid level to model long-range relationships and enhance feature representation. This allows the model to effectively capture contextual information across different scales, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. We evaluate PMT on benchmark medical image segmentation datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN-based and transformer-based methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed pyramid structure and transformer integration in achieving precise and robust medical image segmentation.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various graph-related tasks. However, many existing GNN architectures treat all nodes and edges equally within a neighborhood, neglecting the rich structural information present in a node's immediate ego-network. This paper introduces Ego-GNNs, a novel framework that explicitly exploits the ego structures within each node's neighborhood to enhance GNN performance. Ego-GNNs leverage the inherent connections and relationships within a node's ego-network, such as cliques, stars, and other recurring motifs, to learn more informative node embeddings. We propose a novel aggregation mechanism that considers the structural properties of the ego-network, allowing the model to differentiate between nodes based on their position and role within the local graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Ego-GNNs on several benchmark datasets for node classification and graph classification, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art GNN models. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating ego-structural information in GNN architectures for a more nuanced and effective representation learning process.
Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) systems have emerged as powerful tools for simplifying and accelerating the development of machine learning models. However, even within AutoML, the selection of the best AutoML system for a given task remains a challenge. This paper introduces "Ensemble Squared," a meta-AutoML system designed to address this problem. Ensemble Squared leverages an ensemble of diverse base AutoML systems, strategically combining their individual predictions to achieve superior performance and robustness. Crucially, the system learns to dynamically weight the contributions of each base AutoML system based on the characteristics of the input data and the performance of the individual systems on similar tasks. We present empirical results demonstrating that Ensemble Squared consistently outperforms individual state-of-the-art AutoML systems across a range of benchmark datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in adapting to diverse data distributions and model complexities. This work offers a novel approach to meta-AutoML, significantly enhancing the accessibility and performance of automated machine learning for a broader audience.
Anomaly detection in attributed networks, where nodes and edges possess feature information, is a challenging task. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle to effectively leverage the complex relationships and feature interactions inherent in such networks. This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection framework based on **One-Class Graph Neural Networks (OCGNN)**. Our approach learns a compact and representative embedding space for normal nodes by training a Graph Neural Network (GNN) using only normal data. This one-class learning paradigm allows the model to capture the underlying structure and feature characteristics of normal nodes, enabling it to distinguish them from anomalous nodes. Specifically, we leverage a GNN architecture to aggregate information from neighboring nodes and features, followed by a one-class objective function that encourages the GNN to map normal nodes close to a central point in the embedding space. Anomaly scores are then computed based on the distance of each node's embedding from this learned center. We evaluate our OCGNN framework on several real-world attributed network datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing anomaly detection methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in capturing the complex dependencies within attributed networks and accurately identifying anomalous nodes.
Local-surrogate explainers, such as LIME and SHAP, have become popular tools for understanding individual predictions made by complex machine learning models. However, the process of selecting and defining the specific explanation objective is often overlooked. This abstract argues that the implicit assumptions and choices made in defining what constitutes a "good" explanation for a single instance significantly impact the resulting explanation and its utility. We highlight the importance of explicitly defining explanation objectives, considering factors such as feature sensitivity, counterfactual reasoning, and user-specific needs. By examining the limitations of current practices and proposing avenues for more nuanced and objective-driven approaches, this work aims to contribute to a more robust and reliable application of local-surrogate explainers, ultimately leading to more trustworthy and actionable insights.
This paper presents a comprehensive performance evaluation of deep generative models for generating hand-written character images. We investigate the ability of various architectures, including Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and their variants, to synthesize realistic and diverse hand-written character images. The evaluation encompasses both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Qualitatively, we visually assess the generated images for clarity, resemblance to real hand-written characters, and the presence of artifacts. Quantitatively, we employ metrics such as Inception Score (IS), Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and pixel-wise similarity to evaluate the quality, diversity, and fidelity of the generated images. Furthermore, we explore the impact of different hyperparameters and training strategies on the performance of these models. The results highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture in generating hand-written character images and provide insights into selecting the most suitable model for specific applications requiring realistic and diverse character generation. Our findings contribute to the advancement of deep generative models for image synthesis and offer a valuable benchmark for future research in this domain.
This paper explores various defect detection techniques applicable to the sewing stages of airbag production. The critical nature of airbag functionality necessitates robust quality control measures to identify and eliminate defects arising during the sewing process. This abstract outlines a review of both traditional and emerging methods for defect detection, including visual inspection, automated optical inspection (AOI), pressure testing, and advanced techniques like machine learning-based image analysis. The paper analyzes the strengths and limitations of each technique in detecting common sewing defects such as skipped stitches, loose threads, misaligned seams, and fabric damage. Furthermore, it discusses the potential for integrating these techniques to create a comprehensive defect detection system that enhances the reliability and safety of airbags, contributing to improved passenger safety outcomes.
This paper introduces Contrastive Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (CMSSA), a novel method for extracting and enhancing shared oscillatory patterns across multiple time series datasets. Building upon the foundation of Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA), CMSSA leverages a contrastive learning framework to identify and amplify the common temporal dynamics present in the input data while simultaneously suppressing noise and dataset-specific variations. By constructing positive and negative pairs based on temporal alignment and dataset membership, CMSSA learns a low-dimensional embedding space that emphasizes the shared underlying oscillatory structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of CMSSA through simulations and real-world applications, showcasing its ability to effectively extract coherent signals, improve pattern recognition, and outperform traditional MSSA in scenarios with high noise levels or heterogeneous datasets. The proposed method offers a robust and versatile approach for analyzing complex multivariate time series data and uncovering hidden shared dynamics.
## Abstract: Lip Reading Sentences in the Wild

Automatic lip reading, also known as visual speech recognition, has traditionally focused on constrained environments with controlled lighting and clear articulation. However, real-world applications demand robustness to variations in speaking style, head pose, illumination, and occlusion. This paper addresses the challenging problem of lip reading sentences "in the wild," where such constraints are absent. We explore techniques for robust feature extraction and sequence modeling that can handle the inherent variability and noise present in uncontrolled video data. We investigate the performance of deep learning architectures, specifically [mention specific architectures like CNNs, RNNs, Transformers if applicable], trained on a novel, large-scale dataset of naturally occurring lip movements extracted from [mention dataset source if applicable]. Our results demonstrate [mention key findings, e.g., improved accuracy compared to existing methods, challenges faced, limitations identified]. We conclude by discussing the potential of our approach for applications such as silent speech interfaces, human-computer interaction in noisy environments, and assistance for individuals with hearing impairments, while also highlighting the ethical considerations surrounding the technology.
We introduce InfoBot, a novel reinforcement learning (RL) agent that leverages the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle for improved transfer and exploration. InfoBot learns a compressed representation of its state that captures only the information relevant to predicting future rewards. This compressed representation promotes transfer learning by disentangling task-specific information from irrelevant sensory details, allowing the agent to generalize more effectively to new environments. Simultaneously, the information bottleneck encourages exploration by forcing the agent to discover and represent only the most important features of the environment, thereby reducing the complexity of the learning problem and enabling more efficient exploration strategies. We evaluate InfoBot on a suite of benchmark RL tasks demonstrating its superior performance compared to standard RL algorithms in both transfer learning and exploration settings. Our results highlight the effectiveness of the information bottleneck as a powerful tool for building robust and efficient RL agents.
This paper explores knowledge distillation techniques to improve the efficiency of 3D object detection by transferring knowledge from a multi-frame to a single-frame detector. Multi-frame detectors leverage temporal information to achieve superior accuracy but suffer from increased computational cost and latency. We propose a novel knowledge distillation framework that enables a lightweight, single-frame detector to learn from a more accurate, multi-frame teacher. Our approach focuses on distilling not only the final detection output but also intermediate features and temporal relationships learned by the teacher network. We evaluate our method on benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant performance gains for the single-frame student detector, achieving comparable accuracy to the multi-frame teacher while maintaining real-time processing speeds. This work offers a practical solution for deploying high-performance 3D object detection in resource-constrained environments by effectively bridging the performance gap between multi-frame and single-frame approaches.
This paper presents a medical pre-diagnosis system designed to assist pathologists in the analysis of breast cancer histopathological images. The system leverages [mention the specific AI/ML techniques used, e.g., deep learning, convolutional neural networks, etc.] to automatically identify key features and patterns indicative of malignancy and benignity within the images. The goal is to provide a pre-diagnosis, highlighting areas of concern and suggesting potential diagnoses, thereby reducing the workload on pathologists and improving the speed and accuracy of cancer detection. The system was trained and validated on a [mention the size and characteristics of the dataset used, e.g., large publicly available dataset, a curated clinical dataset etc.] and achieved [mention key performance metrics, e.g., accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC] in distinguishing between different classes of breast cancer. The results demonstrate the potential of this system to serve as a valuable tool for early detection and improved patient outcomes by facilitating faster and more efficient histopathological analysis. Future work will focus on [mention future research directions, e.g., incorporating clinical data, improving interpretability, integrating with existing clinical workflows].
Persistence diagrams are topological summaries that capture the evolution of topological features in data. While powerful, their representation as sets of points in the plane presents challenges for traditional data analysis techniques. Clustering persistence diagrams is a crucial task for tasks like shape classification and data exploration. This work explores the application of Fuzzy c-Means (FCM) clustering to persistence diagrams. By leveraging the flexibility of FCM, we aim to address the inherent uncertainty in assigning diagrams to specific clusters, particularly when diagrams exhibit features that bridge multiple groups. We introduce a novel approach for adapting FCM to the space of persistence diagrams by incorporating appropriate distance metrics, such as the bottleneck or Wasserstein distance, within the FCM objective function. Furthermore, we propose strategies for handling potential issues arising from the non-Euclidean nature of these distance metrics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to identify meaningful clusters within collections of persistence diagrams and provide a more nuanced understanding of the underlying topological structure. Our results suggest that FCM offers a promising framework for clustering persistence diagrams, providing a valuable tool for topological data analysis.
This paper introduces RelGAN, a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture for multi-domain image-to-image translation that leverages **relative attributes** to achieve fine-grained control over image generation. Unlike existing methods that rely on categorical domain labels, RelGAN utilizes continuous attribute vectors representing relative differences between source and target domains. This allows for smooth and controllable transitions between domains, enabling users to specify the degree and direction of change in specific attributes. The proposed architecture incorporates a novel discriminator that evaluates the realism of both the generated images and the consistency of the relative attribute differences between the source and target images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RelGAN on several challenging datasets, showcasing its ability to generate high-quality and diverse images while providing intuitive and fine-grained control over attribute manipulation. Experimental results demonstrate that RelGAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of image quality, attribute control, and perceptual realism.
Ultrasound video offers a wealth of diagnostic information, but its interpretation is often subjective and requires extensive training. This work explores self-supervised representation learning techniques to extract meaningful and robust features directly from unlabeled ultrasound video data. By leveraging inherent structural information within the videos, we aim to learn representations that capture spatiotemporal dynamics and anatomical features without relying on costly manual annotations. We investigate various pretext tasks, including [mention specific pretext tasks like frame order prediction, video colorization, or contrastive learning], to train a deep neural network to encode ultrasound videos into informative feature vectors. We evaluate the learned representations by transferring them to downstream tasks such as [mention potential downstream tasks like pathology classification, frame segmentation, or motion tracking]. Our results demonstrate that self-supervised pre-training significantly improves performance on these tasks compared to training from scratch, highlighting the potential of this approach to reduce annotation burden and improve the accuracy and efficiency of ultrasound video analysis. This work contributes to the development of more accessible and automated ultrasound-based diagnostic tools.
Referring Expression Comprehension (REC), the task of identifying a specific object in an image based on a natural language description, is a fundamental problem in vision-language understanding. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of existing methods and datasets for REC. We categorize and analyze the diverse approaches employed, including attention mechanisms, grounding models, and contextual reasoning techniques, highlighting their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, we present a detailed analysis of publicly available REC datasets, focusing on their characteristics, biases, and suitability for different research objectives. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future research directions in the field, such as improving robustness to ambiguous expressions, incorporating commonsense knowledge, and developing models capable of handling more complex and nuanced language. This survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in REC and its related areas.
Pose-guided person image generation and animation aims to synthesize realistic images of individuals in novel poses, given a source appearance and a target pose. This task presents a significant challenge due to large pose variations and the need to preserve identity details. We propose a novel deep spatial transformation network that effectively handles these challenges. Our approach leverages a two-stage process: first, a pose estimation network predicts the keypoints of the target pose. Then, a deep spatial transformation module warps the source image based on the pose difference, employing a learned dense displacement field to align the source appearance with the target pose. This transformation allows for accurate transfer of textural details and avoids distortions often seen in traditional warping methods. Finally, a generative adversarial network (GAN) refines the warped image, hallucinating missing regions and ensuring photorealistic output. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of visual quality, pose accuracy, and identity preservation, leading to more realistic and controllable person image generation and animation.
Understanding the complex interactions within many-body systems is crucial for predicting and controlling their emergent properties. However, identifying the most relevant interactions from the vast network of possible connections remains a significant challenge. This work introduces a novel geometric attention mechanism specifically designed to detect and prioritize the interactions that "matter" in such systems. Our approach leverages the inherent geometric structure of the system, allowing the model to learn which spatial relationships and orientations are most indicative of strong or influential interactions. By incorporating geometric features into an attention framework, we enable the model to selectively focus on the most important connections between particles, atoms, or other constituents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark tasks, showing that it can accurately identify key interactions, improve predictive accuracy, and provide valuable insights into the underlying physics of many-body systems. This geometric attention mechanism offers a powerful tool for analyzing and understanding complex interactions in a wide range of scientific domains.
This paper proposes a novel contrastive learning framework for learning robust and informative audio-visual representations by leveraging both global and local perspectives. We argue that holistic scene understanding requires capturing both the overall context (global representation) and fine-grained details (local representations) within audio-visual data. Our approach jointly learns these representations by maximizing the agreement between corresponding audio and visual features at both global and local scales, while simultaneously minimizing the agreement between unrelated pairs. Specifically, we employ a multi-branch architecture to extract global features representing the entire audio and visual streams, and local features capturing segment-level information. These features are then projected into a shared embedding space and optimized using a contrastive loss function. By aligning representations across modalities at both global and local levels, our model learns more discriminative and transferable features, leading to improved performance on downstream audio-visual tasks such as event classification, action recognition, and cross-modal retrieval. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showing significant performance gains compared to existing methods that primarily focus on global representations or treat modalities independently.
This paper introduces the Deep Hierarchical Machine (DHM), a novel and flexible machine learning architecture built upon the principle of divide-and-conquer. The DHM decomposes complex problems into a hierarchy of simpler sub-problems, enabling efficient learning and improved generalization. Each level of the hierarchy consists of specialized modules that process specific aspects of the input, and these modules are interconnected in a tree-like structure. This hierarchical decomposition allows for the discovery of meaningful features at different levels of abstraction, leading to a more interpretable and robust model. We demonstrate the flexibility of the DHM by applying it to diverse tasks, highlighting its ability to adapt to varying data complexities and structural dependencies. Experimental results show that the DHM achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while offering advantages in terms of modularity, interpretability, and potential for transfer learning. The proposed architecture provides a promising framework for tackling complex machine learning problems by leveraging the power of hierarchical decomposition and specialized module learning.
This paper investigates the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to develop human-like driving policies for self-driving cars, specifically focusing on collision avoidance tasks. The goal is to train autonomous vehicles that not only avoid collisions but also exhibit driving behaviors that are intuitive and comfortable for human passengers and surrounding traffic. We propose a DRL framework that incorporates a reward function designed to incentivize both safety and human-like driving characteristics, such as smooth lane changes and reasonable speed adjustments. The proposed approach is evaluated in simulated environments featuring complex traffic scenarios and challenging collision avoidance situations. Results demonstrate that our DRL agent learns driving policies that effectively prevent collisions while exhibiting more natural and predictable behaviors compared to traditional rule-based or purely safety-optimized DRL approaches. This work contributes to the development of more acceptable and trustworthy autonomous driving systems by bridging the gap between safety and human-like driving performance.
This paper explores the potential of deep learning to provide enhanced walking assistance for visually impaired individuals. We propose a novel vision-based system, "Vision," that leverages deep neural networks to analyze real-time visual data captured through a wearable camera.  Our approach utilizes [mention specific deep learning architectures, e.g., convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for object detection and semantic segmentation, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for scene understanding] to identify and classify potential obstacles, hazards, and landmarks in the user's environment. This information is then processed to generate navigational cues and alerts, delivered through [mention modality, e.g., haptic feedback, audio cues], enabling safer and more independent navigation. We present preliminary results demonstrating the system's ability to accurately detect and classify common obstacles like sidewalks, stairs, and pedestrians in various environments.  This research aims to contribute towards developing a robust and reliable vision-based assistive technology that empowers visually impaired individuals to navigate their surroundings with greater confidence and independence.
Detecting distress in asphalt pavements is crucial for timely maintenance and ensuring road safety. This paper presents a novel approach utilizing a weightless neural network (WLNN) combined with transfer learning to efficiently and accurately identify asphalt distress. WLNNs offer advantages such as rapid training and low computational cost compared to traditional deep learning models. We leverage transfer learning by adapting pre-trained features from a convolutional neural network (CNN) to the WLNN architecture. This allows us to capitalize on the feature extraction capabilities of CNNs trained on large datasets, while maintaining the efficiency of WLNNs for classification. The proposed method is evaluated on a publicly available asphalt pavement distress dataset, demonstrating significant improvements in classification accuracy and training speed compared to traditional WLNNs and other benchmark methods. The results highlight the potential of this approach for real-time, resource-constrained deployment in automated pavement inspection systems.
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, from game playing to robotics. However, its increasing adoption raises significant security concerns. This paper, "The Faults in Our Pi Stars: Security Issues and Open Challenges in Deep Reinforcement Learning," delves into the vulnerabilities and potential exploits facing DRL agents. We explore a range of attack vectors, including adversarial perturbations, poisoning attacks, and backdoor insertions, highlighting their impact on agent performance and robustness. Furthermore, we identify key open challenges in securing DRL systems, such as the lack of formal verification methods, the difficulty in detecting subtle adversarial manipulations, and the need for more robust training algorithms. By outlining these critical issues, we aim to stimulate further research and development towards building more secure and reliable DRL agents for real-world applications.
Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) offers the potential for sample-efficient learning by leveraging learned models of the environment. However, the accuracy of these learned models is crucial for effective policy optimization. Model errors, particularly compounding errors over long horizons, can lead to suboptimal policies and poor performance. This work introduces a novel framework for **self-correcting models** in MBRL, designed to actively mitigate the impact of model inaccuracies during planning. Our approach focuses on identifying and correcting for model biases by learning a **correction function** that predicts the discrepancy between the model's predictions and the true environment transitions. This correction function is integrated into the planning process, allowing the agent to anticipate and compensate for known model errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our self-correcting models in several challenging continuous control tasks, showing that they significantly improve performance and robustness compared to traditional MBRL methods, particularly in environments with complex dynamics and noisy observations. Our results highlight the importance of explicitly addressing model errors and suggest a promising direction for enhancing the reliability and applicability of MBRL algorithms.
This paper explores the application of deep optics for improving monocular depth estimation and 3D object detection. By jointly optimizing optical element design and deep neural network architectures, we leverage the physical properties of light to encode scene information directly into the captured image. This approach, termed "deep optics," allows us to overcome limitations inherent in traditional single-view geometry and learned depth cues. We present a novel end-to-end framework that co-designs a diffractive optical element (DOE) and a convolutional neural network (CNN) to enhance depth perception from a single RGB image. Our results demonstrate that the engineered optical aberrations, when decoded by the optimized CNN, lead to significant improvements in both depth estimation accuracy and 3D object detection performance compared to traditional lens systems and state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we analyze the learned optical designs to understand how they contribute to improved scene understanding and discuss the potential for future research in integrated optical-neural systems for 3D perception.
Predicting interactions between novel proteins, for which limited experimental data exists, remains a significant challenge in proteomics. Traditional methods often struggle with this cold-start problem due to the lack of known interaction partners. This work proposes a novel approach, **Learning Unknown from Correlations (LUC)**, leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to predict inter-novel-protein interactions. LUC operates on a heterogeneous graph representing proteins and their known interactions, incorporating protein sequence information and functional annotations as node features.  Crucially, LUC exploits the inherent correlations within the interaction network, learning to infer interaction probabilities based on the connectivity patterns and feature similarities surrounding the novel proteins. By aggregating information from known protein-protein interactions and propagating it through the graph, LUC effectively "learns" about the unknown by analyzing the relationships between known and novel proteins.
